Incorrect. The infant rats did learn the association; they just forgot it within days. And the reminder experiment shows the learning was still stored, so this choice gets the problem wrong: it is about keeping access to memories, not about forming them.

Correct. The infant-trained rats seemed to forget, yet after a reminder they acted on the old association, and the control shows the reminder alone couldn't produce that. So the memory wasn't erased; it was stored but out of reach. The choice says this carefully ('need not mean', 'may persist') without repeating the passage's details.

passage.text: Ostrich eggshell beads—small disks cut, drilled, and ground from fragments of shell—have been made in southern and eastern Africa for at least 50,000 years. Comparing more than 1,500 beads from sites across both regions, Jennifer Miller and Yiming Wang found that between roughly 50,000 and 33,000 years ago, beads from sites as much as 3,000 kilometers apart were strikingly similar in diameter and in the width of their central holes, after which the two regions' beads diverged. Because bead styles in many recent African societies serve as markers of shared identity among groups linked by networks of exchange, the researchers concluded that the early similarity reflects sustained social contact between the two regions' populations—contact that shifts in climate later interrupted.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the researchers' conclusion?
choices: Unfinished beads and fragments of drilled shell found at sites in both regions indicate that the beads at each site were manufactured locally.
Beads from sites within each region became more varied in diameter after 33,000 years ago than they had been before that time.
Modern bead makers unfamiliar with ancient beads, using only tools available 40,000 years ago, made beads in the same narrow range of sizes.
Climate records indicate that a broad belt of arid land expanded between the two regions beginning roughly 33,000 years ago.

explanation.passage: The researchers found that, for about 17,000 years, beads from two distant regions had very similar sizes, and later they stopped matching. Their conclusion: the similarity shows the two populations were in contact and shared bead styles, until climate change cut them off. To weaken this, you need a different reason the beads would match, one that doesn't involve contact. The strongest weakener shows the evidence fits that other explanation just as well.
choices: Incorrect. This is the most tempting distractor, because it shows the beads weren't carried from one region to the other. But the conclusion is about social contact and shared identity markers, not about trading the beads themselves. Groups in contact can copy each other's styles and still make their beads at home, so local manufacture is fully consistent with the conclusion.

Incorrect. More variety within each region after 33,000 years ago is about differences inside a region. It doesn't affect the argument, which compares the two regions, and if anything it fits the idea that older shared conventions broke down.

Correct. If people with no knowledge of the ancient beads, using the old tools, end up with the same sizes, then the matching sizes could come from what the materials and tools allow rather than from shared conventions. That gives the similarity an explanation that needs no contact at all, which breaks the link between the evidence and the conclusion.

Incorrect. This supports the conclusion. An arid barrier spreading between the regions around 33,000 years ago fits the researchers' claim that climate shifts interrupted contact at the time the beads diverged.

passage.text: Grid cells in the brain's entorhinal cortex fire in a hexagonal pattern as an animal moves through its surroundings, furnishing a kind of internal coordinate system. Alexandra Constantinescu and colleagues trained participants to associate stylized birds with combinations of two features—neck length and leg length—so that each bird occupied a position in an abstract two-dimensional “space” of shapes; participants then imagined birds morphing continuously in various “directions” through that space while their brains were scanned. The researchers hypothesized that the brain organizes such conceptual knowledge with the same grid-like code it uses for physical space and that this code helps people reason about how concepts relate to one another.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' hypothesis?
choices: As participants imagined the birds morphing, entorhinal activity showed a sixfold directional pattern, strongest in those who best judged how new birds related to familiar ones.
As participants imagined the birds morphing, entorhinal activity varied with the direction of change in a sixfold pattern like that recorded during navigation of physical space.
Participants who most accurately found their way through a virtual town also showed the strongest sixfold pattern of entorhinal activity while moving through that town.
Participants who learned the birds' features fastest best judged how new birds related to familiar ones, whatever the pattern of their entorhinal activity.

explanation.passage: Grid cells act like a map grid for physical space. The researchers created an imaginary 'space' of bird shapes and asked whether the brain maps it the same way. Their hypothesis has two parts: (1) the brain uses the same grid-like code for this abstract space, and (2) that code helps people reason about how concepts relate. Supporting the whole hypothesis takes a finding that backs both parts. A 'sixfold pattern' is the brain-scan signature of grid cells, because a hexagon has six-way symmetry.
choices: Correct. The sixfold pattern during imagined morphing shows the grid-like code is used for the abstract space (part 1). The pattern being strongest in the people who reasoned best about new birds links the code to reasoning (part 2). This is the only choice that covers both parts.

Incorrect. This is the strongest distractor. It gives good evidence for part 1, the grid-like code appearing in the conceptual space, but it says nothing about whether the code helps people reason about how concepts relate. It covers only half of the hypothesis.

Incorrect. This links the grid code to skill, but in a virtual town, which is a physical-style space. The hypothesis is about conceptual knowledge, and grid cells are already known to support spatial navigation, so this finding doesn't test anything new.
Incorrect. This covers reasoning about the birds but explicitly cuts the link to entorhinal activity ('whatever the pattern'). If anything, it suggests the grid code isn't what drives good reasoning.

passage.text: *Jane Eyre* is an 1847 novel by Charlotte Brontë. Recalling her time as a governess at Thornfield Hall, Jane presents her restlessness not as a peculiarity of her own temperament but as one instance of a discontent that is common but seldom voiced, as when she writes, ______

question: Which quotation from *Jane Eyre* most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: “Who blames me? Many, no doubt; and I shall be called discontented. I could not help it: the restlessness was in my nature; it agitated me to pain sometimes.”
“Millions are condemned to a stiller doom than mine, and millions are in silent revolt against their lot.”
“I desired more of practical experience than I then had; more of intercourse with my kind, of acquaintance with variety of character, than was here within my reach.”
“Do you think, because I am poor, obscure, plain, and little, I am soulless and heartless? You think wrong!”

explanation.passage: The claim has two parts. Jane's restlessness is (1) not just a personal quirk but one example of a discontent that is (2) common, felt by many people, yet seldom voiced, meaning those people rarely say it aloud. The right quotation must connect her own situation to many others who feel the same and keep quiet about it. Quotations that describe only Jane's own longings, however vividly, don't make this point.
choices: Incorrect. This is a strong trap, because it is about restlessness by name. But it does the opposite of what the claim needs: it presents the restlessness as personal ('in my nature'). The claim says Jane treats it as more than a peculiarity of her temperament.

Correct. 'Millions are condemned to a stiller doom than mine' places Jane's situation among a great many others (common), and 'in silent revolt against their lot' shows that their discontent goes unspoken (seldom voiced). The quotation never uses the word 'restlessness'; you have to see that a 'stiller doom' is the same confinement Jane chafes against.

Incorrect. This is the other main trap: it comes from the same Thornfield passage and describes exactly what Jane longs for (more experience, more company, more variety of people). But every part of it is about her own desires ('I desired… than was here within my reach'). It never suggests that anyone else shares the discontent or keeps it quiet.

Incorrect. This defends Jane's equal worth despite being poor and plain, so it does suggest she shares something with others. But what she claims to share is a soul and a heart, not a discontent with a confined life, and it is spoken aloud in anger to one person, not a common feeling that goes unvoiced.

passage.text: Cahokia, the largest city in pre-Columbian North America, stood near present-day St. Louis and was largely abandoned by about 1350 CE. A long-standing explanation holds that its inhabitants, by clearing upland forests for fuel and construction timber, increased runoff into nearby Cahokia Creek, so that ever more frequent floods buried the floodplain fields on which the city depended for food. Geoarchaeologist Caitlin Rankin and colleagues, however, reject this explanation.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly explain why Rankin and colleagues reject the common explanation presented in the text?
choices: Pollen preserved in lake sediments near Cahokia shows that upland forest cover declined sharply during the period of the city's most rapid growth.
Wooden palisades enclosing the center of Cahokia were rebuilt several times, and each rebuilding required many thousands of logs.
Floods along the Mississippi River near St. Louis have become more frequent since the 1800s as land in the area has been developed.
Soil layers beside Cahokia Creek record a ground surface that stayed intact, without flood-laid sediment, until long after the city emptied.

explanation.passage: The common explanation is a chain: people cut down upland forests, so more rainwater ran off into the creek, so floods kept burying the fields, so the city lost its food and was abandoned. Rankin's team rejects it. A finding that explains the rejection should break a link in that chain. The most direct break would show that the floods never happened.
choices: Incorrect. This supports the first link of the chain, that forests were cleared. It gives Rankin's team a reason to accept part of the explanation, not to reject it.
Incorrect. This shows Cahokians used a lot of timber, which also supports the deforestation part of the explanation. It doesn't challenge the claim that clearing led to floods.
Incorrect. This is about floods in modern times, after development in the 1800s. It says nothing about whether floods buried Cahokia's fields before 1350.

Correct. If the land beside the creek stayed stable, with no flood deposits, from the city's height until long after it was abandoned, then the floods the explanation depends on didn't bury the floodplain. That breaks the final link of the chain, which is why the researchers would reject it.

passage.text: In a trial run by Lena Ostrowski, patients with chronic low back pain or with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) received no treatment, an “open-label” placebo—pills they were told contained no active ingredient—or a deceptive placebo presented as a new medication. Because such symptoms often ease on their own, Ostrowski counts a treatment's effect as clinically meaningful only if the reduction in symptom score it produces exceeds the reduction in the no-treatment group with the same condition by at least 10 points. She concludes that, for both conditions, deceiving patients is unnecessary for obtaining a clinically meaningful placebo effect.

figure.title: Reduction in Symptom Score after Three Weeks

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that weaken Ostrowski's conclusion?
choices: Among patients with IBS, the open-label placebo reduced symptom scores by 19 points, which was only 7 points more than no treatment did.
For both of the conditions, the deceptive placebo produced a larger reduction in symptom scores than the open-label placebo did.
Among patients with IBS, the deceptive placebo reduced symptom scores by 30 points, which was 11 points more than the open-label placebo did.
Among patients with low back pain, the open-label placebo reduced symptom scores by 21 points, which was 13 points more than no treatment did.

explanation.passage: Ostrowski's rule: an effect is 'clinically meaningful' only if it beats the no-treatment group for the same condition by at least 10 points. Her conclusion is that the open-label placebo (no deception) is meaningful for both conditions. To weaken it, find a condition where the open-label placebo fails the 10-point test. Back pain: open-label 21 minus no treatment 8 = 13, which passes. IBS: open-label 19 minus no treatment 12 = 7, which fails. Note that her conclusion doesn't say open-label works as well as deception, only that deception isn't needed for a meaningful effect.
choices: Correct. For IBS, the open-label placebo beat no treatment by only 19 − 12 = 7 points, below the 10-point threshold. So for IBS, the placebo without deception was not clinically meaningful, which contradicts Ostrowski's claim about both conditions.

Incorrect. This is accurate (24 > 21 and 30 > 19), but it doesn't weaken the conclusion. Ostrowski doesn't claim open-label placebos work as well as deceptive ones, only that deception isn't needed to reach a meaningful effect. A smaller effect can still be meaningful.

Incorrect. The numbers are right, and 11 is above 10, which makes this look like a use of the threshold. But the threshold compares a treatment with no treatment, not one placebo with another. This is the wrong-comparison trap.
Incorrect. This is accurate, but it supports the conclusion: for back pain, the open-label placebo passes the 10-point test (13 points).

passage.text: Whether cattle herding in the Sahara arose as a response to the region's drying has long been debated. At a cluster of rock shelters in the central Sahara, archaeologists measured the share of cattle among identified animal bones and, in sediments from a nearby lakebed, the share of pollen from savanna trees, a proxy for rainfall. Palynologists working in the region treat a fall in savanna-tree pollen below 20 percent of all pollen as marking the onset of aridification, and the archaeologists consider cattle dominant in the local economy once they make up more than half of the identified bones. A student claims that, at these shelters, cattle herding became dominant before aridification began.

figure.title: Cattle Bones and Savanna-Tree Pollen at Central Saharan Sites

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support the student's claim?
choices: Cattle made up 41% of the identified bones 7,000 years ago, when savanna-tree pollen still accounted for 29% of all pollen.
From 9,000 to 4,000 years ago, the share of cattle bones rose from 5% to 80%, while savanna-tree pollen fell from 34% to 9%.
Cattle made up 57% of the identified bones 6,000 years ago, when savanna-tree pollen still accounted for 24% of all pollen.
Savanna-tree pollen fell by 7 points from 6,000 to 5,000 years ago, more than in any other interval, as cattle rose to 72%.

explanation.passage: The passage gives two thresholds you need. Cattle are 'dominant' when they are more than 50% of identified bones. Aridification (drying) begins when savanna-tree pollen falls below 20%. The student claims the first happened before the second. In the graph, cattle first pass 50% at 6,000 years ago (57%). Pollen first falls below 20% at 5,000 years ago (17%). So you need a choice showing cattle above 50% at a time when pollen was still at or above 20%.
choices: Incorrect. This uses the wrong threshold. At 41%, cattle were not yet 'more than half' of the bones, so they weren't dominant by the archaeologists' definition. The choice shows cattle rising while it was still wet, but not that they had become dominant.

Incorrect. This accurately describes both trends, but it says nothing about timing: it doesn't show which threshold was crossed first. Two trends moving in opposite directions over 5,000 years could also fit the idea that drying pushed people into herding.

Correct. At 6,000 years ago, cattle were 57% of the bones, above the 50% mark for dominance, while savanna-tree pollen was 24%, above the 20% mark, so aridification hadn't begun. Cattle dominance came first, as the student claims.

Incorrect. The numbers are accurate (24 − 17 = 7, the largest drop), but this links the rise in cattle to the sharpest drying, which suggests the two happened together. That fits the drying-caused-herding view better than the student's claim.

passage.text: Memory athletes, who can memorize long lists of random words in minutes, typically rely on the “method of loci,” mentally placing each item at a point along a familiar route. Martin Dresler and colleagues trained ordinary adults for six weeks in this method, in a working-memory computer game (an active control), or not at all (a passive control), and tested word recall before training, just after it, and four months later. The researchers classify a group's improvement as durable if, four months after training, the group retains at least half of the gain in words recalled that it showed just after training. A student claims that the method-of-loci group was the only group whose improvement was durable.

figure.title: Mean Number of Words Recalled (out of 72)

question: Which choice best describes the extent to which the data in the table support the student's claim?
choices: The data support the claim, because the method-of-loci group recalled 48 words four months after training, far more than either of the other groups did.
The data do not support the claim, because four months after training the method-of-loci group recalled 14 fewer words than it had just after training.
The data support the claim, because the working-memory group had retained only 1 of the 7 additional words it recalled just after training.
The data do not support the claim, because the group that received no training also retained more than half of its gain at four months.

explanation.passage: The passage defines 'durable': at four months, a group keeps at least half of the gain it made just after training. Gain = 'just after' minus 'before'. Retained = 'four months' minus 'before'. Method of loci: gain 62 − 26 = 36, retained 48 − 26 = 22, and 22 is more than half of 36 (18), so durable. Working-memory game: gain 35 − 28 = 7, retained 29 − 28 = 1, less than 3.5, so not durable. No training: gain 31 − 27 = 4, retained 30 − 27 = 3, more than 2, so durable by the definition, even though the gain is tiny. The student says only the loci group was durable, so check every group.
choices: Incorrect. This compares raw recall at four months instead of applying the durability test, which is about how much of each group's own gain was kept. Recalling the most words doesn't make the loci group the only durable one.

Incorrect. This misreads the definition. A group doesn't have to keep all of its gain, only at least half. The loci group kept 22 of its 36-word gain, more than half, so its improvement was durable despite the 14-word drop.

Incorrect. This is accurate for the working-memory group (it kept 1 of 7), but it checks only one of the two other groups. The no-training group, which this choice skips, passes the test. This is the incomplete-check trap.

Correct. The no-training group gained 4 words (27 to 31) and kept 3 of them at four months (30), more than half. By the researchers' definition, its improvement was durable too, so the loci group was not the only durable one, even though its gain was far larger.

passage.text: Do people who reflect professionally on ethics behave better than others? Philosophers Eric Schwitzgebel and Joshua Rust surveyed professional ethicists, philosophers in other fields, and professors outside philosophy, asking whether eating the meat of mammals is morally bad and whether they had eaten such meat at their most recent evening meal. The researchers reasoned that if moral reflection shapes conduct, then a group's greater readiness to condemn the practice should be matched by a comparably lower rate of engaging in it. They concluded that ethicists' conduct did not reflect their views to the extent this reasoning predicts, at least when ethicists are compared with other philosophers.

figure.title: Views on and Consumption of Mammal Meat

series.name: Say eating mammal meat is morally bad
Ate mammal meat at most recent evening meal

figure.note: Non-philosophers are professors in fields outside philosophy.

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Schwitzgebel and Rust's conclusion?
choices: Ethicists were less likely than either of the other two groups to report having eaten mammal meat at their most recent evening meal.
Ethicists were 15 points likelier than other philosophers to call eating mammal meat morally bad but only 2 points less likely to have eaten it.
Professors outside philosophy were the least likely of the three groups to call eating mammal meat morally bad and the most likely to report having eaten it.
More than a third of the respondents in each of the three groups reported having eaten mammal meat at their most recent evening meal.

explanation.passage: The researchers' test: if thinking about ethics changes behavior, a group that condemns meat-eating much more often should also eat meat much less often. Their conclusion is about ethicists compared with other philosophers. So compare those two groups on both bars. Condemning: ethicists 60%, other philosophers 45%, a 15-point gap. Eating: ethicists 38%, other philosophers 40%, only a 2-point gap. The behavior gap is far smaller than the opinion gap.
choices: Incorrect. This is accurate (38% versus 40% and 46%), but it points the wrong way: ethicists eating meat least often is what you'd expect if moral reflection does shape conduct. It doesn't show the mismatch the researchers concluded.

Correct. A 15-point difference in condemning the practice is matched by only a 2-point difference in doing it. That is exactly the failure of 'comparable' change in behavior that the conclusion describes, for the comparison it names: ethicists and other philosophers.

Incorrect. This is accurate (19% condemn, 46% ate), but it shows views and behavior lining up, which supports the idea that views shape conduct. It also concerns the wrong comparison; the conclusion is about ethicists and other philosophers.
Incorrect. True for every group (38%, 40%, 46%), but it doesn't compare views with behavior, so it can't show whether behavior matched views.

intro: The following text is adapted from Herman Melville's 1853 story “Bartleby, the Scrivener.” The narrator, a New York lawyer, is describing himself. John Jacob Astor was a famously wealthy American businessman.

passage.text: I am a man who, from his youth upwards, has been filled with a profound conviction that the easiest way of life is the best. Hence, though I belong to a profession proverbially energetic and nervous, even to turbulence, at times, yet nothing of that sort have I ever suffered to invade my peace. I am one of those unambitious lawyers who never addresses a jury, or in any way draws down public applause; but in the cool tranquillity of a snug retreat, do a snug business among rich men's bonds and mortgages and title-deeds. All who know me consider me an eminently safe man. The late John Jacob Astor, a personage little given to poetic enthusiasm, had no hesitation in pronouncing my first grand point to be prudence; my next, method. I do not speak it in vanity, but simply record the fact, that I was not unemployed in my profession by the late John Jacob Astor; a name which, I admit, I love to repeat, for it hath a rounded and orbicular sound to it, and rings like unto bullion [gold or silver in bars].

question: Which choice best describes how the narrator is presented in the text?
choices: As a man who modestly declines to boast of his own achievements, preferring to let the praise of a respected client speak for him
As a man who, despite his reputation for prudence, privately longs for the public acclaim that more ambitious lawyers enjoy
As a man whose professed indifference to distinction is belied by the evident relish he takes in a wealthy man's regard
As a man whose devotion to an easy life has led him to neglect the demands of a profession he considers turbulent

explanation.passage: The narrator says he loves an easy, quiet life and is an 'unambitious' lawyer who avoids public applause. Then he spends several sentences on the fact that the famously rich John Jacob Astor praised him and employed him. He insists 'I do not speak it in vanity', yet admits he loves to repeat Astor's name because it 'rings like unto bullion' (sounds like gold). That gap between what he says about himself and what he obviously enjoys is the irony. The question asks how the text presents him, so you need to catch what Melville shows, not only what the narrator claims.
choices: Incorrect. This takes the narrator at his word ('I do not speak it in vanity'). But he goes out of his way to mention Astor's praise and confesses that he loves repeating Astor's name for its golden sound. Letting a famous client's praise 'speak for him' is itself a way of boasting, and the text makes the vanity show.

Incorrect. This is half right: there is a hidden appetite for distinction. But nothing suggests he wants public acclaim; he seems content to avoid juries and applause. What he relishes is a rich man's private approval, not the crowd's. The 'longs for public acclaim' part is unsupported.

Correct. He claims to be 'unambitious' and to shun applause, yet he lingers on Astor's praise and loves to repeat Astor's name because it 'rings like unto bullion'. His pleasure in a wealthy man's approval gives the lie to ('belies') his modest self-description. The choice names that contradiction without repeating the passage's words.

Incorrect. He keeps the turbulence of his profession out of his life by choosing a quiet kind of work, but he doesn't neglect his duties. He does 'a snug business' and is praised for 'prudence' and 'method'. This turns his preference for calm into a failing the passage never shows.

passage.text: In a brief passage of his 1739 *Treatise of Human Nature*, David Hume observed that moral writers proceed for some time in the ordinary way of reasoning, describing what is, and then, imperceptibly, begin to assert what ought to be—a shift for which, he wrote, “a reason should be given.” Generations of philosophers have read the passage as establishing an unbridgeable gap: no conclusion about obligation can ever be derived from facts alone. Yet Hume's own moral theory grounds virtue and vice in facts about the sentiments of approval and disapproval that human beings reliably feel, and several recent commentators have therefore proposed that the passage is better understood as a demand that moralists make explicit the steps by which they pass from description to prescription than as a prohibition on their doing so.

question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: A celebrated philosophical passage may have been read as making a stronger claim than its author, judging by his other commitments, intended.
Hume's moral theory, which derives virtue and vice from human feelings, contradicts the rule he set out in a famous passage of his *Treatise*.
Recent commentators have shown that conclusions about obligation can legitimately be derived from facts about how human beings feel.
Philosophers have long misread Hume because the passage in question is too brief to convey his position on moral reasoning clearly.

explanation.passage: Hume noticed that writers on morality move from statements about what is to statements about what ought to be, and he said a reason should be given for that move. Most philosophers read this as a ban: you can never get an 'ought' from an 'is'. The passage then points out a problem with that reading. Hume's own theory bases morality on facts about human feelings, which would break the ban. So recent commentators suggest he was only asking writers to explain the move, not forbidding it. The main idea is about how the famous passage should be interpreted.
choices: Correct. The 'celebrated passage' is Hume's, the 'stronger claim' is the ban on deriving ought from is, and 'judging by his other commitments' refers to his sentiment-based moral theory, the evidence commentators use. The hedge 'may have been read' matches 'proposed'. The choice never says 'is' or 'ought', so you have to recognize the paraphrase.

Incorrect. This accepts the traditional reading, which the passage questions. If the famous passage only asks for an explanation, Hume's theory doesn't contradict it. The commentators use the apparent conflict as a reason to reread the passage, not as a charge against Hume.

Incorrect. Too strong, and the wrong kind of claim. The commentators make a proposal about what Hume meant; they don't 'show' that moral conclusions can be derived from facts. The passage is about interpreting a text, not settling the philosophical question.

Incorrect. The passage notes the passage is 'brief', but it never blames the misreading on brevity. The reason it gives for rereading Hume is the conflict with his moral theory. This adds a cause the text doesn't state.

passage.text: When bronzes of extraordinary intricacy—vessels and regalia cast with delicate tracery and tiny modeled insects—were excavated at Igbo-Ukwu in southeastern Nigeria and dated to the ninth or tenth century CE, some European scholars insisted that so refined a technique must have been introduced from outside Africa. Metallurgical analyses have since shown that the bronzes are made of an alloy, rich in lead and silver, that is unknown in contemporary Mediterranean or Islamic metalwork and consistent with ores from deposits roughly a hundred kilometers from the site. The same burials, however, held tens of thousands of glass beads, many of which chemical analysis traces to workshops in Egypt and possibly India—evidence that Igbo-Ukwu was tied into exchange networks spanning much of the Old World.

question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The glass beads found at Igbo-Ukwu suggest that the techniques used to cast its bronzes probably arrived through long-distance exchange.
Scholars' assumptions about Igbo-Ukwu's bronzes have been overturned by evidence that the site had little contact with the Mediterranean world.
The intricacy of Igbo-Ukwu's bronzes has led scholars to reconsider when the site first began to take part in Old World exchange networks.
Evidence indicates that Igbo-Ukwu's metalwork was a local achievement, though the community was by no means isolated from distant regions.

explanation.passage: Some European scholars assumed the Igbo-Ukwu bronzes were too sophisticated to be African and must have come from elsewhere. Metal analysis shows otherwise: the alloy matches nothing in Mediterranean or Islamic metalwork and fits nearby ores, so the bronzes were made locally. The last sentence adds a twist with 'however': the same burials had glass beads from Egypt and perhaps India, so the community did trade far away. A main-idea answer must hold both points: local metalwork, and long-distance connections.
choices: Incorrect. This uses the beads to support the old assumption the passage rejects. The beads show that trade existed, but the metal analysis shows the bronzes themselves are unlike foreign metalwork and fit local ores. The choice runs the passage's evidence in the wrong direction.

Incorrect. Half right: the assumption about the bronzes was overturned. But the beads came partly from Egypt, and the passage says Igbo-Ukwu was tied into networks spanning much of the Old World. The passage never claims the site had little contact with distant places; it says the opposite.

Incorrect. This recycles words from the passage ('intricacy', 'exchange networks') in a claim it never makes. Nothing is said about scholars revising when the trade began, and the intricacy of the bronzes isn't connected to dating anything.

Correct. The alloy analysis shows the bronzes were made locally, refuting the outside-origin claim, and the beads show the community still had far-reaching trade. 'By no means isolated' is an understated way of saying it was linked to distant regions, and the choice avoids naming the beads or the alloy.

intro: The following text is adapted from Emily Brontë's 1847 novel *Wuthering Heights*. The narrator, Mr. Lockwood, has recently rented a house from Mr. Heathcliff in a remote part of northern England.

passage.text: 1801.—I have just returned from a visit to my landlord—the solitary neighbour that I shall be troubled with. This is certainly a beautiful country! In all England, I do not believe that I could have fixed on a situation so completely removed from the stir of society. A perfect misanthropist's [person who dislikes humankind] heaven: and Mr. Heathcliff and I are such a suitable pair to divide the desolation between us. A capital fellow! He little imagined how my heart warmed towards him when I beheld his black eyes withdraw so suspiciously under their brows, as I rode up, and when his fingers sheltered themselves, with a jealous resolution, still further in his waistcoat, as I announced my name.

question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To depict the start of a friendship between two men who are drawn together by their shared and settled preference for solitude
To introduce a narrator whose enthusiasm for a new acquaintance sits oddly with the unwelcoming conduct he describes
To establish the remoteness of the setting as the cause of the hostility that the narrator's new neighbor displays
To show a narrator concealing his resentment of a neighbor's rudeness beneath a display of exaggerated praise

explanation.passage: Lockwood, the narrator, has just met his landlord, Heathcliff. He is delighted with the lonely countryside and decides that he and Heathcliff are a perfect pair of loners. He calls Heathcliff 'A capital fellow!' (a splendid man). But look at what he actually describes: Heathcliff's eyes 'withdraw so suspiciously', and he keeps his hands 'with a jealous resolution' in his waistcoat instead of offering a handshake. Heathcliff is plainly unfriendly, yet Lockwood says his 'heart warmed towards him'. The question asks what the passage is mainly doing.
choices: Incorrect. This takes Lockwood's view at face value. He calls them 'a suitable pair', but the only behavior shown is Heathcliff's suspicion and refusal to shake hands. Nothing suggests Heathcliff feels any friendship; the passage invites us to doubt Lockwood's reading.

Correct. Lockwood is warm and enthusiastic ('A capital fellow!', 'my heart warmed'), but the details he reports, suspicious eyes and hands kept away from him, show a cold reception. The passage's purpose is to present a narrator whose judgment doesn't match his own evidence. 'Sits oddly with' is understated, and the choice avoids the passage's distinctive words.

Incorrect. The passage stresses the setting's remoteness, but only as something Lockwood enjoys. It never says the isolation makes Heathcliff hostile. This adds a cause-and-effect link the text doesn't make.

Incorrect. This reads Lockwood's praise as sarcasm. But nothing shows that he resents Heathcliff; he says his heart 'warmed' and seems pleased to have found a fellow loner. The irony comes from the author, at Lockwood's expense, not from Lockwood hiding his feelings.

passage.text: In experiments begun in the early 1980s, Benjamin Libet found that a slow buildup of electrical activity in the brain—the “readiness potential”—began several hundred milliseconds before participants reported having decided to flex a wrist, a result widely taken to show that the brain initiates actions before conscious will does. In 2012, Aaron Schurger and colleagues proposed that the buildup need not reflect any decision at all: if spontaneous neural activity fluctuates randomly and a movement occurs whenever it happens to cross a threshold, then averaging many recordings aligned to the moment of movement—as Libet did—would produce a gradual rise even though no process had been steadily preparing the act. Schurger's model does not show that conscious will initiates action; it removes, rather, one of the chief reasons for thinking that it does not.

question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It presents a finding, identifies a flaw in the method used to obtain it, and then argues that the finding should be replaced by new evidence that conscious will initiates action.
It describes a debate between two researchers, evaluates the evidence that each offers, and then concludes that the role of conscious will cannot be settled by experiment.
It presents a finding and a popular reading of it, describes an account under which the finding would arise without supporting that reading, and then clarifies that account's limited force.
It presents a finding and a popular reading of it, describes a model that calls the finding's accuracy into doubt, and then concedes that the popular reading nonetheless remains the most plausible.

explanation.passage: Sentence 1 gives Libet's finding (brain activity builds up before people feel they decide) and the popular interpretation (the brain starts actions before conscious will). Sentence 2 gives Schurger's alternative: random brain activity plus averaging would create the same buildup with no decision behind it. Sentence 3 is careful about what this shows: it doesn't prove conscious will starts actions; it only removes a main argument against that. The question asks you to describe these three moves.
choices: Incorrect. The last step is wrong. The text explicitly says Schurger's model 'does not show that conscious will initiates action'. It never argues for replacing Libet's finding with evidence for conscious will. The first two steps are close enough to make this tempting.

Incorrect. The text doesn't stage a debate or weigh the researchers' evidence against each other, and it doesn't conclude that experiments can't settle the question. That last step is a much broader claim than the text's narrow point about one argument.

Correct. 'A finding and a popular reading' is Libet's result and the claim that the brain acts before will. 'An account under which the finding would arise without supporting that reading' is Schurger's random-fluctuation model. 'Clarifies that account's limited force' is the final sentence: it removes a reason, but proves nothing about will.

Incorrect. Two steps are off. Schurger's model doesn't doubt that the buildup is real; it reinterprets what the buildup means. And the text doesn't concede that Libet's popular reading is still most plausible; it says the model removes one of the main reasons for that reading.

passage.label: Text 1
passage.text: Neuroimaging studies led by Nancy Kanwisher identified a small region of the brain's fusiform gyrus that responds far more strongly to faces than to houses, hands, or other objects. Because the response is so selective, and because damage near the region can impair face recognition while leaving object recognition largely intact, Kanwisher and others have argued that the region is a module dedicated specifically to processing faces.

passage.label: Text 2
passage.text: Isabel Gauthier and colleagues found that in people with extensive expertise in identifying birds or cars, the same fusiform region responds to those objects nearly as strongly as to faces, and that novices trained over several weeks to tell apart individual members of a family of novel computer-generated objects called “Greebles” show a growing response to them there. Faces, Gauthier notes, are simply the one category that virtually everyone spends a lifetime learning to distinguish individual by individual.

question: Based on the texts, how would Gauthier (Text 2) most likely respond to the argument presented in Text 1?
choices: By suggesting that the region's selectivity may reflect a general capacity for expert discrimination among similar items, not a dedication to faces
By arguing that once people have been trained to recognize Greebles, the region responds no more strongly at all to faces than it does to other objects
By contending that damage near the region impairs the recognition of birds and cars by experts as severely as it impairs the recognition of faces
By agreeing that the region is dedicated to faces but proposing that expertise with other objects is developed in a neighboring area of the brain

explanation.passage: Text 1: a brain region responds much more to faces than to other things, so Kanwisher argues it is built just for faces. Text 2: in bird and car experts, the same region responds to birds or cars almost as much as to faces, and training people to tell apart made-up objects (Greebles) increases the region's response to them. Gauthier adds that faces are the one category everyone becomes an expert at. Put together: the region may be for telling apart similar things you're expert in, and faces are just the most common case.
choices: Correct. Text 2 shows the region responds to any category a person has learned to tell apart individual by individual, and it explains faces as the universal case of such expertise. So Gauthier would say the face selectivity may come from expertise rather than a face-only module. The hedge 'may reflect' fits her evidence.

Incorrect. Too strong. Training produced a 'growing response' to Greebles, not a response equal to faces. Even the experts' response to birds or cars was only 'nearly as strong' as to faces. Text 2 never claims faces lose their special status.
Incorrect. Text 2 says nothing about brain damage. This invents evidence to answer the second part of Kanwisher's argument, which Gauthier doesn't address.

Incorrect. This contradicts Text 2, which says expertise with birds, cars and Greebles activates 'the same fusiform region', not a neighboring area. Gauthier challenges the idea that the region is dedicated to faces rather than agreeing with it.

passage.label: Text 1
passage.text: Serpent Mound, a quarter-mile-long earthwork in southern Ohio shaped like an undulating snake, was long attributed to the Adena culture, which flourished in the region from about 800 BCE to 100 CE. In 1991, however, excavators recovered charcoal from within the mound that yielded radiocarbon dates of around 1070 CE, and they concluded that the effigy had been built by the much later Fort Ancient culture.

passage.label: Text 2
passage.text: In 2014, Edward Herrmann and colleagues extracted sediment cores at several points along the serpent's body, including the undisturbed soil directly beneath it. Charcoal from the earliest construction layers dated to roughly 300 BCE. The team also found signs that parts of the mound had been disturbed and repaired over the centuries—work that could have introduced younger material into the earthwork long after it was first raised.

question: Based on the texts, how would Herrmann and colleagues (Text 2) most likely respond to the conclusion drawn by the excavators in Text 1?
choices: By arguing that the mound was raised around 300 BCE and then left untouched until it was studied in modern times.
By contending that the Fort Ancient people had no involvement with Serpent Mound at any point in the earthwork's long history
By proposing that the Adena and Fort Ancient cultures each constructed separate portions of the serpent's body at widely different times
By suggesting that the material the excavators dated may record a later episode of activity at the mound rather than its construction

explanation.passage: Text 1: Serpent Mound was thought to be Adena (800 BCE–100 CE), but in 1991 charcoal from inside the mound dated to about 1070 CE, so excavators credited the later Fort Ancient culture. Text 2: new cores found charcoal in the earliest building layers dating to about 300 BCE, which is in the Adena period. Text 2 also found the mound had been repaired over time, and repairs can add younger material. Combine them: the 1991 charcoal may come from a later repair rather than from the original building.
choices: Incorrect. Half right: Text 2 does date the earliest construction to around 300 BCE. But Text 2 also says parts of the mound 'had been disturbed and repaired over the centuries', so it was not left untouched. Those repairs are exactly what lets Text 2 explain the 1991 dates.

Incorrect. Too strong. Text 2 says the mound was repaired over the centuries, possibly long after it was built, and the 1070 CE charcoal could come from such work. That leaves room for later people, possibly Fort Ancient, to have worked on it. Text 2 doesn't rule out their involvement.

Incorrect. Over-specified. Text 2 mentions repairs to parts of an existing mound, not separate construction of different sections by two cultures. The earliest construction layers date to about 300 BCE.

Correct. Text 2 dates the earliest construction to around 300 BCE and notes that later repairs could have introduced younger material. So the 1991 charcoal (around 1070 CE) may reflect later work on the mound, not when it was built. The choice is hedged ('may record') and doesn't name either culture.

passage.label: Text 1
passage.text: In a 1972 essay, philosopher Peter Singer asked readers to imagine walking past a shallow pond in which a child is drowning. Nearly everyone agrees that one ought to wade in and save the child, even at the cost of ruining one's clothes. Singer argued that the principle underlying this verdict—if we can prevent something very bad without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to do it—obliges the affluent to give much of their income to relieve poverty in distant countries.

passage.label: Text 2
passage.text: The force of the pond case derives in part from its singularity: the emergency is sudden, it ends once the child is pulled out, and the rescuer may then return to the rest of life. Global poverty is chronic. A principle that demanded rescue whenever rescue was possible would, applied to an emergency that never ends, leave no part of a person's life outside its reach. Our confident verdict about the pond may thus attest to a duty to answer occasional emergencies, not to the far more demanding one that is inferred from it.

question: Based on the texts, the author of Text 2 would most likely agree with which statement about the pond example discussed in Text 1?
choices: It is misleading, because the distance between a rescuer and a person in need is morally relevant, whereas Singer treats it as irrelevant.
The judgment it elicits may support a less extensive obligation than the one Singer uses it to justify for the affluent.
It shows that people have no obligation to help others in need except when an emergency is both sudden and brief.
It succeeds in establishing Singer's principle, though the principle should apply to poverty only when giving costs little.

explanation.passage: Text 1: everyone agrees you should save a drowning child even if it ruins your clothes, and Singer says the same principle means wealthy people should give much of their income to fight distant poverty. Text 2 doesn't deny we should save the child. It argues the pond case feels so clear because it is a one-time emergency that ends. Poverty never ends, so a principle requiring rescue every time would take over your whole life. Text 2 concludes that the pond verdict may only show a duty to help in occasional emergencies, a smaller duty than Singer's.
choices: Incorrect. This is the best-known objection to Singer, which makes it tempting, but Text 2 never mentions distance. Its point is about how long the emergency lasts (sudden and ending versus chronic), not how far away the person in need is.

Correct. Text 2 says our verdict about the pond 'may… attest to a duty to answer occasional emergencies, not to the far more demanding one' Singer draws. In other words, the intuition supports a narrower obligation than Singer's conclusion. The choice keeps Text 2's hedge and avoids its wording.

Incorrect. Too strong. Text 2 says the pond verdict may support only a duty to answer occasional emergencies, but it doesn't say that is the only obligation people have. It questions what the example proves; it doesn't deny every other duty to help.

Incorrect. Text 2 doesn't accept that the pond case establishes Singer's principle. It argues the principle, applied to a never-ending emergency, would demand too much, and it suggests the pond verdict supports something narrower. The 'costs little' limit is not in Text 2.

passage.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 1982, philosopher Frank Jackson published a thought experiment about a scientist he called Mary.
• Mary knows every physical fact about color vision but has spent her entire life in a black-and-white room.
• When Mary leaves the room and sees a red tomato, she seems to learn something new: what it is like to see red.
• From this, Jackson concluded that some facts about conscious experience are not physical facts.
• In 1974, philosopher Robert Nozick had imagined an “experience machine” that could give a person any pleasant experience.
• Nozick argued that because most people would refuse to plug into the machine, people must value more than pleasant experiences.

question: The student wants to present Jackson's thought experiment and the conclusion he drew from it to an audience unfamiliar with the thought experiment. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: In a 1982 thought experiment, Frank Jackson imagined Mary, a scientist raised in a black-and-white room who knows every physical fact about color vision.
Like Nozick's earlier “experience machine,” Jackson's 1982 thought experiment led its author to conclude that experience involves more than physical facts.
Jackson held that since a scientist who knew every physical fact about color but had never seen it would learn something by seeing red, not all facts are physical.
When Jackson's Mary sees a red tomato for the first time, she learns what it is like to see red, which led Jackson to conclude that some facts about experience are not physical.

explanation.passage: The goal has two parts: (1) present the thought experiment and Jackson's conclusion, and (2) do it for readers who have never heard of it. So the sentence must explain what makes Mary's case work (she already knows every physical fact about color but has never seen color) and then state the conclusion (some facts about experience aren't physical). All four choices are accurate to the notes or close to it, so check each against both parts.
choices: Incorrect. This sets up the scenario clearly for a new reader, but it stops there. It never says what happens when Mary sees red or what Jackson concluded, so it presents only half of what the goal asks for.

Incorrect. This states a conclusion but never describes the thought experiment, so an unfamiliar reader learns nothing about Mary. It also wrongly gives Nozick the same conclusion; according to the notes, Nozick concluded that people value more than pleasant experiences, not that some facts aren't physical.

Correct. It explains the setup an unfamiliar reader needs (a scientist who knows every physical fact about color but has never seen it), what happens (she learns something on seeing red), and Jackson's conclusion (not all facts are physical). Both parts of the goal are met.

Incorrect. This is the strongest distractor: it describes the key moment and states the conclusion. But 'Jackson's Mary' assumes the reader already knows who Mary is, and it leaves out the crucial detail that she already knew every physical fact about color. Without that detail, an unfamiliar reader can't see why learning what red looks like shows that some facts aren't physical.

passage.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Inca Empire (c. 1400–1532) kept records on khipus.
• A khipu is a set of knotted cords hanging from a main cord; the type and position of the knots encode numbers.
• Scholars have long debated whether khipus also recorded information other than numbers.
• Manuel Medrano compared six khipus from Peru's Santa valley with a Spanish colonial census of the same community.
• He found that the cords' colors and the way they were tied to the main cord matched the census's names and social groups.
• This suggests that khipus encoded some non-numerical information, such as membership in a social group.

question: The student wants to emphasize the significance of Medrano's finding for an audience unfamiliar with khipus. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Medrano's matching of six khipus (Inca records of cords whose knots encode numbers) to a census suggests that khipus also held non-numerical data.
A khipu, a record kept by the Inca Empire, is a set of knotted cords hanging from a main cord, with the type and position of the knots encoding numbers.
Medrano's comparison suggests that khipus encoded some non-numerical information, such as social group membership, a question that scholars had long debated.
Medrano compared six khipus from Peru's Santa valley with a Spanish colonial census of the same community, focusing on the cords' colors and attachment.

explanation.passage: Two conditions here. (1) Emphasize why Medrano's finding matters: khipus, long known to record numbers, seem to have recorded other information too, which settles part of a long debate. (2) The audience doesn't know what a khipu is, so the sentence has to explain it briefly. Check each choice for both.
choices: Correct. The parenthesis explains what a khipu is (cords whose knots encode numbers), and the point that khipus 'also held non-numerical data' shows why the finding matters: it goes beyond the numbers khipus were known to record. The hedge 'suggests' matches the notes. Both conditions are met.
Incorrect. This explains khipus well, meeting the audience condition, but it never mentions Medrano's finding, so it can't emphasize its significance.

Incorrect. This is the closest distractor. It states the finding with the same hedge as the notes and even signals its importance by mentioning the long debate. But it never explains what a khipu is, so a reader unfamiliar with them can't follow why encoding names would matter. It fails only the audience condition.
Incorrect. This describes what Medrano did (his method) but not what he found or why it matters, and it doesn't explain what a khipu is.

passage.text: Participants in a large study led by Adrian Owen who practiced commercial “brain-training” games for six weeks improved markedly on the games themselves. On untrained tests of reasoning, memory, and planning, however, they performed no better than a control group that had spent the same time answering general-knowledge questions online. ______ what the training had produced was proficiency at the particular tasks practiced, not an enhancement of the underlying capacities those tasks were designed to exercise.

question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: That said,
In effect,
By the same token,
Even so,

explanation.passage: Sentence 1: players got much better at the games. Sentence 2, with 'however': they did no better than the control group on other tests. The sentence with the blank sums up what those two results mean together: the training made people good at the games, not smarter in general. So the blank must introduce a summary of the overall upshot, not a new contrast. The contrast has already been made with 'however'.
choices: Incorrect. 'That said' introduces a qualification of what came before, a 'but' point. The final sentence doesn't qualify sentence 2; it states what sentences 1 and 2 add up to. A reader who sees the final sentence mention something the training 'had produced' may treat it as a partial defense of the games, but it is actually the conclusion that the games don't build general abilities.

Correct. 'In effect' introduces a statement of what something amounts to. Sentences 1 and 2 show improvement on the games but not on untrained tests, and the final sentence states what that amounts to: skill at the specific tasks, not better underlying abilities.
Incorrect. 'By the same token' introduces a parallel case that follows the same logic. The final sentence isn't a second, similar case; it interprets the same study.

Incorrect. 'Even so' means 'despite that'. The final sentence doesn't hold true in spite of the participants' poor results on untrained tests; it follows from them. This trap works if you link the blank to sentence 1's improvement and skip sentence 2.

passage.text: Most people hold that an agent can be blamed only for what lies within his or her control; yet, as philosopher Thomas Nagel observed, we routinely judge a drunk driver who kills a pedestrian more harshly than an equally reckless one who, by sheer luck, arrives home without incident. ______ we admire a rescuer who pulls a swimmer from a riptide more than one who makes an identical attempt but is swept back by a wave. In both pairs, an outcome that neither agent controlled appears to alter our assessment of the agent.

question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: In contrast,
Indeed,
Notwithstanding this,
By the same token,

explanation.passage: Sentence 1 sets up a puzzle. We say people should be blamed only for what they control, yet we blame the drunk driver who kills someone more than the equally reckless driver who got lucky. The outcome is a matter of luck, but it changes our judgment. The sentence with the blank gives the same pattern for praise: two rescuers try equally hard, and we admire the one who succeeds more. The last sentence confirms that both pairs show the same thing. So the blank must signal a parallel example.
choices: Incorrect. This is the main trap. Blame and admiration are opposites, so the two examples can look like a contrast. But the logical relationship is a parallel: in both, luck changes our judgment. The final sentence ('In both pairs…') confirms the examples work the same way.

Incorrect. 'Indeed' introduces a point that reinforces or intensifies the previous claim, often a stronger restatement of it. The rescuer sentence isn't a stronger version of the driver example; it is a separate, parallel case from a different area (praise rather than blame). The blank needs a word that marks a second case working by the same logic.
Incorrect. 'Notwithstanding this' introduces something true despite what came before. The rescuer example doesn't push against the driver example; it supports the same point.
Correct. 'By the same token' means 'for the same reason' or 'in the same way'. It introduces a second case that works by the same logic as the first: luck affects praise just as it affects blame.

intro: The following text is from Herman Melville's 1853 story “Bartleby, the Scrivener.” The narrator, a lawyer, is describing the first days of work of a copyist he has recently hired.

passage.text: At first Bartleby did an extraordinary quantity of writing. As if long famishing for something to copy, he seemed to gorge himself on my documents. There was no pause for digestion. He ran a day and night line, copying by sun-light and by candle-light. I should have been quite delighted with his [u]application[/u], had he been cheerfully industrious. But he wrote on silently, palely, mechanically.

question: As used in the text, what does the word “application” most nearly mean?
choices: Request
Diligence
Appetite
Relevance

explanation.passage: The narrator, a lawyer, describes his new copyist, Bartleby. Bartleby copies an enormous amount, day and night. The narrator uses an eating image ('famishing', 'gorge', 'digestion') to show how hungrily he works. Then the narrator says he would have been delighted with Bartleby's 'application' if Bartleby had been 'cheerfully industrious'. That phrase is the clue: 'application' is the hard work itself, and 'cheerfully industrious' names what it lacked, cheerfulness. The final sentence shows the work was done 'silently, palely, mechanically'.
choices: Incorrect. This is the everyday meaning, as in a job application. But Bartleby has already been hired, and the sentence is about how he works, not about anything he asked for.

Correct. 'Application' here means steady, hard effort, as in 'applying oneself'. Bartleby copies 'day and night', and the narrator would have been delighted with this effort had it come with cheerfulness ('cheerfully industrious'). Diligence fits that meaning exactly.

Incorrect. This is the mood trap. The passage's eating images ('famishing', 'gorge') make 'appetite' feel right. But those images are a comparison describing how Bartleby works; the narrator is delighted with the work itself, which he links to being 'industrious', not with a hunger.

Incorrect. This draws on another sense of 'application', how well something applies to a situation, as in 'a rule's application to this case'. Nothing in the sentence concerns whether Bartleby or his work is relevant to anything.

passage.text: Maya blue, a pigment used across Mesoamerica from about 800 CE, has survived centuries of tropical humidity and resists even boiling nitric acid, which destroys ordinary indigo within minutes. The pigment combines indigo with palygorskite, a clay whose crystals are threaded with narrow parallel tunnels normally filled with loosely held water, and its durability has generally been credited to indigo molecules lodged deep inside those tunnels, sealed off from attack. Reproducing the pigment, chemist Marisol Duarte found that heating an indigo–clay mixture to 150°C—hot enough to drive out the water, and so make room for indigo, in the outermost portion of each tunnel but not in its interior—yielded a product as acid-resistant as ancient samples. That resistance, moreover, was lost once the product's indigo content exceeded about 1 percent by weight, a small fraction of what the tunnels' full volume could hold. Together, these findings suggest that ______

question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: Maya artisans must have heated their pigment to about 150°C, since no other temperature would have yielded comparable resistance to acid.
the water remaining in the interior of each tunnel, rather than the clay or the indigo, is what protects the finished pigment from acid.
the pigment's durability may not require that indigo molecules make their way very far into the clay's tunnels.
the tunnels can protect only a limited amount of indigo, so pigments richer in indigo would be darker but more easily damaged.

explanation.passage: Maya blue is indigo dye mixed with a clay (palygorskite) whose crystals contain tiny tunnels full of water. The usual explanation for its toughness is that indigo sits deep inside the tunnels, where acid can't reach it. Duarte's two findings both cut against 'deep inside'. First, heating that empties only the outer ends of the tunnels (the inner parts keep their water) is enough to make a fully resistant pigment, so the indigo had room to enter only near the tunnel openings. Second, the clay can protect only a tiny amount of indigo, far less than the whole tunnels could hold, which again points to a limited set of sites near the openings. The question asks what both findings together suggest about the traditional 'deep inside' explanation.
choices: Incorrect. This is over-specified. Duarte showed that 150°C works; she didn't test other temperatures or show that nothing else could work. The passage also says nothing about the temperatures Maya artisans actually used, so 'must have' and 'no other temperature' go well beyond the evidence.

Incorrect. This recycles the passage's detail about water left inside the tunnels and turns it into a new mechanism. The passage mentions the interior water only to show where indigo could not have gone; it never says the water protects anything. Ordinary indigo is destroyed by acid, and nothing suggests water would shield it.

Correct. If heating empties only the outer ends of the tunnels and still produces a fully durable pigment, the indigo needed to go no deeper than those ends. The 1 percent limit, a small fraction of the full tunnel volume, fits the same picture: only a few sites near the openings protect indigo. Both findings challenge the idea that durability comes from indigo 'lodged deep inside'. The answer is hedged ('may not require') and doesn't repeat the passage's wording.

Incorrect. This is the half-right trap. The first part fits the second finding (only a small amount of indigo is protected), and 'more easily damaged' is reasonable. But 'darker' is an unsupported add-on: the passage never discusses color. The choice also ignores the first finding, so it misses what the two findings suggest together.

passage.text: Because California randomizes the order in which candidates' names appear on its ballots, political scientists can measure the advantage, if any, that comes from being listed first. Studies of the state's elections have found that advantage to be substantial in party primaries, where every candidate in a contest shares the same party label, but negligible for partisan offices in general elections. One interpretation holds that primary voters, being fewer and less engaged, are simply more prone to defaulting to the first name they see. Yet on general-election ballots—cast by the very electorate that produced negligible effects for partisan offices—the advantage reappears, at magnitudes comparable to those in primaries, in contests for nonpartisan posts such as county judge, which are listed without party labels. This pattern suggests that ______

question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the size of the advantage reflects differences among the contests on a ballot more than differences among the voters casting it.
primary voters are more likely than general-election voters to choose whichever name is listed first, regardless of the office being contested.
adding party labels to nonpartisan contests would eliminate the first-position advantage that candidates in those contests currently enjoy.
candidates in nonpartisan contests gain more from being listed first in general elections than candidates in party primaries gain from it.

explanation.passage: Because California shuffles the order of names, researchers can see whether being listed first helps. It helps a lot in primaries and hardly at all for partisan offices in general elections. One explanation blames the voters: primary voters are less engaged and just pick the first name. The last sentence tests that explanation. The same general-election voters who ignored ballot order for partisan offices did show the first-name advantage, about as strongly as in primaries, for nonpartisan offices listed without party labels. So the same people behave differently depending on the contest. What the passage is building toward is that the contest, not the type of voter, drives the effect.
choices: Correct. The same general-election voters show almost no first-name effect in partisan contests but a primary-sized effect in nonpartisan ones. Since the voters are the same, the difference must come from something about the contests, and the passage hints at what: whether a party label is shown. This choice states that conclusion abstractly without repeating 'party label' or 'nonpartisan'.

Incorrect. This restates the 'less engaged primary voters' interpretation, which the passage introduces only to undercut it with 'Yet'. The general-election evidence shows that the voters supposedly less prone to the effect display it fully in nonpartisan contests, so the difference isn't about who votes.

Incorrect. This is an overreach. The pattern is consistent with party labels mattering, but no one tested adding labels to nonpartisan races, and 'eliminate' is much stronger than anything the evidence shows. The passage supports a general conclusion about contests, not a confident prediction about a policy change.

Incorrect. This misreads a comparison. The passage says the general-election advantage in nonpartisan contests appears 'at magnitudes comparable to those in primaries', meaning about the same size, not larger.

passage.text: Until the mid-1920s, nearly all motion pictures were shot on orthochromatic film, a stock highly sensitive to blue light but almost blind to red. Blue objects thus registered on it nearly as brightly as white ones, and red objects nearly as darkly as black ones—a property studios learned to exploit: costume records from the period indicate that shirts appearing brilliant white on screen were often dyed pale blue, because truly white fabric reflected so much light that it bloomed into a blurred halo. Some digital restorations now add color to such films, assigning each object a hue according to how light or dark it appears in the surviving footage. Film historian Ines Haldane argues that this practice ______

question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: would be reliable for blue and white objects but not for red ones, which the film rendered almost as darkly as black.
rests on an assumption about how tone corresponds to color that footage of this kind does not dependably satisfy.
should give way to the methods of hand-coloring that studios themselves used before the mid-1920s.
is undermined chiefly by the halo effect, which blurred white objects so badly that their colors cannot be identified.

explanation.passage: Old 'orthochromatic' film saw blue very well and red hardly at all. So on screen, blue looked almost white and red looked almost black. Studios used this on purpose: a shirt that looks white in the film was often pale blue in real life, because real white fabric glowed too much. Modern colorizers guess an object's color from how light or dark it looks in the black-and-white footage. Put the two facts together. If a pale blue shirt shows up as white and a red dress shows up as nearly black, then lightness in this footage is a poor guide to the real color. That is what Haldane's argument should say.
choices: Incorrect. This is the strongest trap, because the passage says red registered almost as black, which would fool a colorizer. But it gets blue backwards: blue registered 'nearly as brightly as white', so a pale blue shirt would be colored white by mistake. The method fails for blue as well as red, not just for red.

Correct. Colorizing by lightness assumes that light objects were light-colored and dark objects dark-colored. On orthochromatic film that assumption breaks: pale blue reads as white, and red reads as nearly black. This choice states the problem abstractly ('how tone corresponds to color'), with no mention of shirts, blue or red, and with a hedge ('does not dependably satisfy').

Incorrect. This adds a recommendation from outside the passage. Nothing mentions studios' own hand-coloring methods, so the passage gives no basis for preferring them. It doesn't follow from the facts about orthochromatic film.

Incorrect. This recycles the 'halo' detail but misuses it. The passage says studios avoided the halo by dyeing white items pale blue, so the halo isn't what misleads colorizers. The real problem is that the substitute blue looks white in the footage.

passage.text: In medieval England, a person accused of a serious crime who could prove he was a member of the clergy was entitled to “benefit of clergy”: transfer to a church court, which could not impose the death penalty. Because clergy were among the few people who could read, the accepted proof of clerical status became the ability to read a passage aloud—usually a verse from Psalm 51, which many defendants simply memorized in advance. A statute of 1489 left this reading test in place but provided that a layman, meaning anyone not in holy orders, could claim the benefit only once, and that he was to be branded on the thumb so that any second claim could be detected. In keeping the reading test while adding this provision, Parliament appears to have ______

question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: sought to restore the privilege to its original purpose by excluding from it every defendant who was not actually in holy orders.
recognized that the reading test had become meaningless, since defendants could pass it by memorizing the verse in advance.
intended the branding chiefly as a punishment for members of the clergy who had claimed the privilege more than once.
tacitly accepted that some who were not clergy would claim the privilege, while limiting how often they could do so.

explanation.passage: 'Benefit of clergy' let an accused clergyman escape the death penalty by being tried in a church court. The proof of being clergy was reading a verse aloud, and since anyone could memorize the verse, ordinary men (laymen) could claim it too. The 1489 law did not get rid of the reading test. Instead, it said a layman could use the benefit once and would be branded so he couldn't use it again. The key detail is the word 'layman': the law openly expects non-clergy to claim the benefit and only limits them to one use.
choices: Incorrect. This is the opposite of what the statute did. It explicitly allowed a layman to claim the benefit once, so it didn't exclude everyone outside holy orders. A careless reader may assume a reform must have tightened the rule completely.

Incorrect. This is the strongest distractor. The passage does say defendants memorized the verse, so the test was easy to beat. But Parliament kept the test, which is hard to square with deciding it was 'meaningless'. The statute limited how often laymen could use the privilege rather than abandoning the test.
Incorrect. Wrong group. The branding provision applies to a layman, 'anyone not in holy orders', and its stated purpose is to detect a second claim, not to punish clergy.

Correct. By writing a rule for laymen who claim the benefit, Parliament acknowledged without saying so that non-clergy would pass the reading test. It responded by capping their use at once, with a brand to enforce the cap. 'Tacitly accepted' captures that unspoken acknowledgment.

passage.text: Cosmetics recovered from ancient Egyptian tombs frequently contain laurionite and phosgenite, two lead chloride compounds that are rare in nature. No Egyptian source of either mineral is known, and chemist Philippe Walter and colleagues showed that both can be produced by soaking lead oxide in salt water and replacing the solution daily for several weeks—a procedure resembling recipes recorded by later Greco-Roman writers. On this basis, the researchers concluded that Egyptian cosmetic makers deliberately synthesized the compounds, which would make the cosmetics evidence of a “wet chemistry” practiced as early as 2000 BCE.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the researchers' conclusion?
choices: Galena and cerussite, the common lead minerals that make up most of the cosmetics, slowly turn into laurionite and phosgenite after centuries in contact with chloride-bearing moisture.
The earliest surviving written description of the salt-water procedure dates to the first century CE, roughly two thousand years after the oldest cosmetics containing the compounds were made.
Some Egyptian cosmetics from the same period contain no laurionite or phosgenite at all, being made entirely of galena and cerussite.
The laurionite and phosgenite crystals in the cosmetics are uniform in size and shape, as is typical of compounds formed by precipitation from a solution rather than ground from ore.

explanation.passage: The researchers' reasoning goes: the cosmetics contain two rare lead compounds; Egypt had no natural source of them; they can be made in the lab with salt water; so Egyptians must have made them on purpose. To weaken this, you want another way the compounds could have ended up in the cosmetics, one that doesn't require ancient chemists. The strongest weakener explains the evidence (the compounds are present) without the conclusion (deliberate synthesis). Watch for choices that seem to question the researchers but leave their core inference standing, and choices that actually help them.
choices: Correct. If the ordinary lead minerals in the cosmetics turn into laurionite and phosgenite on their own after centuries in damp, salty conditions, the compounds may have formed in the tomb long after the cosmetics were made. Their presence then no longer shows that anyone synthesized them. This weakens the conclusion indirectly by offering an equally good explanation for the same evidence.

Incorrect. This is the main trap. It sounds damaging because the written recipe is much later than the cosmetics. But the researchers' case doesn't rest on the recipe being contemporary. It rests on the rare compounds being present with no natural source, and on lab work showing they can be made. A late record leaves that inference intact; it only means the method went undocumented for a long time.

Incorrect. This is true-but-not-the-task. Some cosmetics lacking the compounds tells you nothing about how the compounds got into the cosmetics that do contain them. It is consistent with deliberate synthesis (makers produced different recipes) and with any other explanation, so it neither offers an alternative source nor breaks the researchers' inference.
Incorrect. This supports the researchers. Crystals typical of precipitation from solution fit the salt-water process they proposed and rule out simply grinding up a natural ore.

passage.text: When U.S. states began adopting legislative term limits in the 1990s, supporters predicted that the limits would produce “citizen legislators” more attentive to voters than to careers in office. Political scientists Lena Brandt and Óscar Ruiz advance a less sanguine view. By forcing members out before they can master the intricacies of budgeting and regulation, term limits, they hypothesize, shift influence over policy away from legislatures and toward governors, whose permanent staffs retain the very expertise that departing legislators take with them.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Brandt and Ruiz's hypothesis?
