That's a different job from supporting her own account, so look for something that is hard to square with printers trying to hide that their books were printed.
choices: Correct. If printers openly announced at the end of their books that the books were printed, they clearly weren't trying to pass them off as handwritten. That directly undercuts the deception explanation, which is what Veit rejects.

Incorrect. This is the main trap. It fits Veit's own idea that typefaces signaled the kind of book. But a printer trying to fool buyers would also copy the script each kind of manuscript used, so this finding doesn't count against the deception explanation. It supports her alternative without explaining why she rejects the old one.
Incorrect. Lower prices for printed copies suggest buyers did value them less, which is the assumption behind the deception explanation. This would support the explanation Veit rejects.

Incorrect. Using the same decorators shows continuity between manuscripts and printed books, but that is equally consistent with deception (it would make printed books look more handwritten) and with Veit's view. It doesn't explain why she rejects the old explanation.

passage.text: Agronomists evaluate intercropping—growing two crops together in one field—with the land equivalent ratio (LER). Each crop's yield in the intercrop is divided by its yield when grown alone, and these two “partial” ratios are summed. An LER above 1.0 means that producing the same harvests in separate fields would require more land, and intercrops that clear this mark are routinely described as advantageous. Agronomist Priya Raman cautions that the label can mislead: an intercrop may exceed 1.0 even though one of its crops yields only a small fraction of its solo harvest, provided the other crop yields nearly as much as it would alone. For farmers who need substantial harvests of both crops, she argues, such an intercrop offers little real advantage.

figure.title: Partial Land Equivalent Ratios in Four Intercrops

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to illustrate Raman's caution?
choices: In the wheat–faba bean intercrop, faba bean's partial LER was just 0.18, even though wheat's partial LER reached 0.78.
The sorghum–pigeon pea intercrop had the highest LER of the four, with partial LERs of 0.85 for sorghum and 0.48 for pigeon pea.
In the barley–pea intercrop, the two crops' partial LERs of 0.55 for barley and 0.60 for pea summed to an LER of 1.15.
In the millet–cowpea intercrop, millet's partial LER of 0.92 and cowpea's of 0.21 summed to an LER of 1.13.

explanation.passage: The LER adds up two fractions: how much of its solo yield each crop produces when the two are grown together. Above 1.0 counts as 'advantageous'. Raman warns about a specific case: the total is above 1.0, but only because one crop does almost as well as alone while the other does poorly. So you need an intercrop that meets both conditions: total above 1.0, and one crop's partial LER near 1 with the other's low. Add each pair of bars before choosing.
choices: Incorrect. This is the threshold trap. Faba bean does poorly (0.18), which looks like Raman's case, but 0.78 + 0.18 = 0.96, which is below 1.0. This intercrop would not be labeled advantageous in the first place, so it can't show that the label misleads.
Incorrect. Sorghum–pigeon pea does have the highest LER (1.33), but both crops do reasonably well. It's an example of a genuine advantage, not of the misleading case Raman describes.

Incorrect. The LER of 1.15 is above 1.0, but the two crops do about equally well (0.55 and 0.60). Neither crop is close to its solo harvest while the other lags far behind, so this doesn't illustrate her caution.

Correct. The total, 1.13, is above 1.0, so this intercrop would be called advantageous. But that total depends on millet doing almost as well as alone (0.92) while cowpea gets only about a fifth of its solo harvest (0.21). For a farmer who needs both crops, that's the misleading case Raman describes.

passage.text: Before the sixteenth century, most books printed in German-speaking cities were in Latin, the language of the church and the universities. Historian Lukas Brenner argues that the Reformation, which began in 1517 and generated a flood of vernacular pamphlets, accelerated rather than initiated the move toward German. German's share of all titles printed in these cities, he contends, was already growing in the years before 1517; the Reformation merely made it grow far faster. To evaluate the argument, a student compiled estimated counts of the titles printed in each language at five-year intervals.

figure.title: Estimated Titles Printed in German-Speaking Cities, by Language

question: Which choice best describes the extent to which the data in the graph support Brenner's argument?
choices: The data support both parts of the argument, since the number of German titles rose in every interval before 1517 and rose far more steeply afterward.
The data support the claim of a post-1517 acceleration but not of an earlier rise, since German titles were a shrinking share of output before 1517.
The data undercut both parts of the argument, since the number of Latin titles grew by more than the number of German titles from 1500 to 1515.
The data support the claim of an earlier rise but not of an acceleration, since German titles did not outnumber Latin titles until after 1520.

explanation.passage: Brenner makes two claims about German's share of all titles, meaning German titles as a fraction of the total. (1) The share was already rising before 1517. (2) It rose much faster after 1517. The graph shows counts, not shares, so you have to work out the shares. 1500: 50 of 250 = 20%. 1505: 60 of 360 ≈ 17%. 1510: 70 of 470 ≈ 15%. 1515: 80 of 580 ≈ 14%. 1520: 400 of 850 ≈ 47%. 1525: 650 of 1,050 ≈ 62%. So the share fell before 1517 and then shot up.
choices: Incorrect. This is the count-versus-share trap. The number of German titles did rise before 1517 (50 to 80), but Latin titles rose much faster (200 to 500), so German's share fell from 20% to about 14%. The first part of Brenner's claim, about share, is not supported.

Correct. Before 1517, German's share dropped from 20% to about 14%, which contradicts the claim that it was already rising. After 1517 it jumped to about 47% and then 62%, which fits the claimed acceleration. So the data support one part and not the other.

Incorrect. The Latin comparison does undercut part 1, which is why this is tempting. But it says nothing about the period after 1517, when German's share soared, so the data don't undercut both parts.

Incorrect. This gets both parts backward. The share fell before 1517, so there was no earlier rise, and it climbed steeply after 1517, so there was an acceleration. When German titles first outnumbered Latin ones doesn't decide either claim.

passage.text: Sociologists have often found that neighborhoods with many homeowners are also neighborhoods where residents know one another, and the pattern is usually attributed to ownership itself: owners, it is said, have a financial stake in their surroundings. Sociologist Hana Okoro suspects instead that ownership matters mainly because owners tend to stay put, and that what fosters acquaintance is length of residence. If ownership mattered in its own right, she reasons, two neighborhoods with similar median lengths of residence but very different proportions of renters should differ markedly in how well residents know their neighbors; yet in her survey of four neighborhoods, ______

figure.title: Survey of Four Neighborhoods
columns: Residents who know 5+ neighbors by name (%)

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: Alder Park and Brookline, whose shares of renters differ by only 2 percentage points, differ by 34 points in the share of residents who know 5+ neighbors.
Cedar Hill, where fewer than a third of residents rent, has a smaller share of residents who know 5+ neighbors than Alder Park, where most residents rent.
Alder Park and Dunmore, with renter shares of 72% and 34% but median residences of 9 and 11 years, have similar shares who know 5+ neighbors.
Dunmore, which has the longest median length of residence of the four neighborhoods, also has the largest share of residents who know 5+ neighbors.

explanation.passage: The usual view is that owning a home makes people get to know their neighbors. Okoro thinks what really matters is how long people have lived there. She sets up a specific test: find two neighborhoods where people have lived about the same length of time but the share of renters is very different. If ownership mattered, those neighborhoods should differ a lot in acquaintance. The sentence begins 'yet', so the blank must show they don't differ much. Find the pair that fits that exact test.
choices: Incorrect. This pair has similar renter shares and different lengths of residence (9 vs. 3 years), the reverse of Okoro's test. It's consistent with her idea, but it doesn't complete her 'yet' sentence, which is about neighborhoods with similar residence lengths and different renter shares.

Incorrect. This comparison seems to cut against ownership, but Cedar Hill's and Alder Park's residence lengths differ a lot (4 vs. 9 years). It doesn't hold residence length steady, so it isn't the comparison Okoro describes.

Correct. Alder Park and Dunmore have similar residence lengths (9 and 11 years) but very different renter shares (72% vs. 34%). If ownership mattered by itself, they should differ markedly, yet their acquaintance figures are close (58% and 61%). That is exactly the result the 'yet' sentence calls for.

Incorrect. This is true and fits Okoro's view in general, but it describes a single neighborhood. It doesn't compare two neighborhoods with similar residence lengths and different renter shares, which is what the sentence requires.

passage.text: Many plants of fire-prone shrublands germinate in response to chemicals in smoke, a trait thought to time germination to the open, nutrient-rich conditions that follow a fire. Ecologist Rosa Delgado hypothesizes that smoke responsiveness has evolved only in species from habitats that burn regularly. To test the idea, she germinated seeds of two species from California chaparral, which burns every few decades, and two from coastal dunes, where fires are virtually unknown, with and without exposure to smoke-treated water. Following convention, she classified a species as smoke-responsive if smoke treatment raised its germination rate by at least 15 percentage points over that of untreated seeds.

figure.title: Germination With and Without Smoke Treatment

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that weaken Delgado's hypothesis?
choices: Germination of Camissoniopsis, a dune species, rose from 18% without smoke treatment to 34% with it.
Germination of Salvia, a chaparral species, rose by only 13 percentage points with smoke treatment, from 30% to 43%.
Germination of Abronia, a dune species, was 55% without smoke treatment, the highest untreated rate of the four.
Germination of Emmenanthe, a chaparral species, rose by 29 percentage points with smoke treatment, the largest increase.

explanation.passage: Delgado's hypothesis uses the word 'only': smoke responsiveness appears only in species from habitats that burn. 'Smoke-responsive' has a set definition: smoke must raise germination by at least 15 percentage points. Chaparral burns; dunes basically never do. To weaken an 'only' claim, you need a smoke-responsive species from the habitat that doesn't burn. A fire-habitat species that isn't responsive doesn't contradict 'only', because she never claimed every fire-habitat species responds.
choices: Correct. Camissoniopsis comes from the dunes, where fires are virtually unknown, yet smoke raised its germination by 16 points (18% to 34%). That meets the 15-point threshold, so a species from a non-burning habitat is smoke-responsive, which contradicts 'only'. You have to do the subtraction and apply the threshold yourself.

Incorrect. This is the main trap. Salvia falls short of the 15-point threshold, so a chaparral species is not smoke-responsive. But Delgado said responsiveness occurs only in fire-prone species, not in all of them. A fire-prone species that doesn't respond is consistent with her hypothesis.

Incorrect. This is accurate, but a high untreated rate says nothing about the effect of smoke. Abronia rose only 3 points (55% to 58%), so it's a non-responsive dune species, which fits the hypothesis.
Incorrect. Emmenanthe is a fire-habitat species with a strong response. That is exactly what the hypothesis expects, so it supports rather than weakens it.

intro: The following text is from Henry James's 1878 novella *Daisy Miller*. Winterbourne is a young American who has lived for many years in Geneva, Switzerland.

passage.text: When his friends spoke of him, they usually said that he was at Geneva “studying.” When his enemies spoke of him, they said—but, after all, he had no enemies; he was an extremely amiable fellow, and universally liked. What I should say is, simply, that when certain persons spoke of him they affirmed that the reason of his spending so much time at Geneva was that he was extremely devoted to a lady who lived there—a foreign lady—a person older than himself. Very few Americans—indeed, I think none—had ever seen this lady, about whom there were some singular stories.

question: Based on the text, what does the narrator most strongly suggest about Winterbourne?
choices: He is so widely liked that even the rumors circulating about his private life are repeated without any hint of disapproval.
He has devoted himself so wholly to his studies in Geneva that he has lost touch with most of his fellow Americans.
The respectable reason given for his long stay in Geneva may be less accurate than a more delicate one the narrator relays.
The narrator doubts the stories told about him, since almost no Americans have ever seen the lady he is said to be devoted to.

explanation.passage: The narrator explains why Winterbourne lives in Geneva. His friends say he is 'studying', and the quotation marks hint that the word is a polite cover. The narrator then starts to report what his enemies say, stops himself and insists he has no enemies, which is a show of tact. Then, 'simply', he reports the rumor anyway: Winterbourne is devoted to an older foreign lady about whom there are 'singular' (odd) stories. The question asks what this sly, roundabout narration suggests about Winterbourne's real reason for staying.
choices: Incorrect. This takes 'he had no enemies… universally liked' at face value. The narrator uses that protest as a polite way to go on and repeat the rumor, and a devotion to an older foreign lady with 'singular stories' attached is hardly reported without a hint of disapproval.
Incorrect. This takes 'studying' literally, ignoring the quotation marks that cast doubt on it. The passage also never says he has lost touch with Americans; it says Americans haven't seen the lady.

Correct. The quotation marks around 'studying' cast doubt on the friends' explanation, and the narrator's pretended reluctance ('but, after all, he had no enemies') sets up a less proper one: devotion to an older foreign lady. The choice captures the irony, the 'respectable' reason that may be a cover, without repeating 'studying' or 'foreign lady'.

Incorrect. The narrator never says he doubts the stories. Noting that hardly any Americans have seen the lady adds mystery and gossip value; it isn't offered as grounds for disbelief. This reads a doubt into the passage that isn't there.

passage.text: For much of the twentieth century, sociologists held that cultural taste mirrored social hierarchy: elites favored opera and classical music and disdained popular forms. In the 1990s, Richard Peterson's surveys suggested that this “snob” had given way to the “omnivore,” a high-status consumer who enjoys a broad range of genres, and many took omnivorousness as evidence of declining cultural exclusivity. Subsequent interview studies complicate that reading. Omnivores, they find, embrace country music or street food chiefly in forms coded as authentic or obscure—an early recording, a family-run stall—while dismissing commercially popular versions of the same genres, and they discuss these preferences in a vocabulary of discernment that few lower-status respondents use. Breadth of taste, on this account, may be less a retreat from distinction than a newer means of displaying it.

question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Research suggests that the broad tastes of high-status consumers may mark social standing rather than show that such marking has waned.
Interview studies have shown that Peterson's surveys overstated how wide a range of genres high-status consumers actually enjoy.
High-status consumers favor obscure versions of popular genres chiefly because they regard commercial culture as aesthetically inferior.
Interview studies show that high-status omnivores describe their preferences in a vocabulary of discernment that lower-status respondents seldom use.

explanation.passage: The old view was that elites liked 'high' culture and looked down on popular culture. In the 1990s, Peterson found that elites now like many kinds of culture (they are 'omnivores'), and many people took this to mean culture had become less exclusive. The interview studies don't dispute that elites' tastes are broad. They question what the breadth means: elites pick the 'authentic' or obscure versions and talk about them in a way that shows refinement. The last sentence gives the main idea: broad taste may be a new way of showing status, not a sign that status display is fading.
choices: Correct. This matches the final sentence: breadth of taste is 'less a retreat from distinction than a newer means of displaying it'. It paraphrases abstractly ('mark social standing', 'such marking has waned') instead of reusing 'distinction' or 'omnivore', and it is hedged with 'may'.

Incorrect. This is tempting because the interview studies 'complicate' Peterson. But they challenge how his finding was interpreted (as declining exclusivity), not the finding itself. The passage accepts that omnivores do enjoy many genres; it questions what that breadth means.

Incorrect. This takes a supporting detail (preferring obscure forms) and adds a motive the passage never gives. The passage's point is that these choices display status, not that omnivores think commercial culture is aesthetically worse. A detail plus an invented motive isn't the main idea.

Incorrect. This is accurate (the passage says omnivores use 'a vocabulary of discernment that few lower-status respondents use'), which makes it tempting. But it is one piece of supporting evidence. The main idea is what that evidence adds up to: breadth of taste may be a new way of displaying status.

passage.text: The semi-dwarf wheat varieties that spread across Asia and Latin America in the 1960s owe their short stature to mutations that make the plants less responsive to gibberellin, a hormone that promotes stem elongation. Their success is often summarized as a matter of higher yields, but the mutations did not, on their own, make wheat more productive: grown on unfertilized land, early semi-dwarfs typically yielded no more than the tall varieties they replaced. What the mutations changed was how the plants responded to nitrogen. Tall wheat given heavy doses of fertilizer grew taller still and tended to topple over—to “lodge”—before harvest, ruining much of the crop, whereas semi-dwarfs channeled the added nitrogen into grain while their short, stiff stems stayed upright.

question: Based on the text, which statement about semi-dwarf wheat is most strongly supported?
choices: Because it is less responsive to gibberellin, it produces more grain than tall wheat regardless of how much nitrogen the soil contains.
It was adopted chiefly in regions where tall wheat had been unable to grow at all without heavy applications of nitrogen fertilizer.
Tall varieties would yield as much as semi-dwarfs on heavily fertilized land if some other means of keeping them upright were found.
Its advantage over the varieties it replaced depended largely on an input that farmers themselves had to supply.

explanation.passage: Semi-dwarf wheat is short because it responds less to a growth hormone. The passage corrects a common story: the mutations didn't make wheat more productive by themselves, because without fertilizer, semi-dwarfs yielded no more than tall wheat. What changed was the response to nitrogen fertilizer. Tall wheat with lots of fertilizer grew taller and fell over, while semi-dwarfs put the nitrogen into grain and stayed standing. So the yield advantage appears only when farmers add fertilizer.
choices: Incorrect. The first half is accurate (the plants respond less to gibberellin), but 'regardless of how much nitrogen' contradicts the passage. On unfertilized land, semi-dwarfs 'yielded no more than' tall varieties.
Incorrect. The passage never says where semi-dwarfs were adopted or that tall wheat couldn't grow without fertilizer. Tall wheat grew fine without it; it fell over only when heavily fertilized.

Incorrect. This is an appealing what-if, but the passage doesn't support it. Fertilized tall wheat 'grew taller still', which suggests its extra nitrogen went into stems rather than grain. Nothing indicates that propping it up would make it match semi-dwarf yields.

Correct. Without fertilizer, semi-dwarfs had no yield advantage; with heavy fertilizer, they turned the nitrogen into grain and didn't fall over. So their advantage depended on fertilizer, an input farmers had to apply. The choice never says 'fertilizer' or 'nitrogen'; you have to recognize 'an input that farmers themselves had to supply' as the same idea.

intro: The following text is Christina Rossetti's 1862 sonnet “Remember.” The speaker addresses someone she loves.

passage.text:
Remember me when I am gone away,
Gone far away into the silent land;
When you can no more hold me by the hand,
Nor I half turn to go yet turning stay.
Remember me when no more day by day
You tell me of our future that you plann'd:
Only remember me; you understand
It will be late to counsel then or pray.
Yet if you should forget me for a while
And afterwards remember, do not grieve:
For if the darkness and corruption leave
A vestige of the thoughts that once I had,
Better by far you should forget and smile
Than that you should remember and be sad.

question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: The speaker asks the listener to remember her and then explains why such remembrance will be of no use to her once she is dead.
The speaker voices a repeated plea and then qualifies it in light of a concern she comes to rank above the plea itself.
The speaker makes a request and then withdraws it entirely, having concluded that remembering the dead always brings grief.
The speaker contrasts the listener's present devotion with the indifference she predicts the listener will soon come to feel.

explanation.passage: The speaker imagines dying ('gone away… into the silent land'). In the first eight lines she asks again and again to be remembered: 'Remember me', 'Remember me', 'Only remember me'. Line 9 turns with 'Yet'. If the listener forgets for a while, she shouldn't grieve, because it is 'better by far' to forget and be happy than to remember and be sad. So the request stands, but the speaker decides the listener's happiness matters more. The question asks for the shape of that movement.
choices: Incorrect. Line 8 does say it will be 'late to counsel then or pray', which makes this tempting. But the poem's turn ('Yet') is not about whether remembrance helps the speaker. It is about the listener's feelings: forgetting and smiling is 'better by far' than remembering and being sad. This misidentifies what the second part of the poem does.

Correct. The first eight lines repeat a plea ('Remember me' three times). After 'Yet', she qualifies it: forgetting is acceptable, even 'better by far', if remembering would make the listener sad. The listener's happiness becomes more important than being remembered. The choice describes this abstractly without quoting the poem.

Incorrect. This is the main trap. The ending does soften the request, but it doesn't withdraw it 'entirely'. She still hopes to be remembered and only prefers forgetting to sad remembering. 'Always brings grief' also overstates; the poem says 'if' remembering would make the listener sad.

Incorrect. The poem imagines the listener might forget 'for a while', but never predicts indifference. It treats forgetting gently, as something to be forgiven, not as coldness to be contrasted with present love.

passage.text: For much of the nineteenth century, new British novels were typically issued in three volumes, and literary historians once took the format as evidence of Victorian readers' appetite for expansive, leisurely narratives. Few readers, however, actually bought these books. Priced at a guinea and a half—more than many workers earned in a week—they were purchased chiefly by circulating libraries such as Mudie's, which lent them to subscribers one volume at a time, so that a single set could serve three borrowers at once. The libraries accordingly pressed publishers to keep both the format and its price in place. When the major libraries refused to go on paying those prices in 1894, the three-volume novel vanished within a few years, although nothing suggests that readers' tastes had changed.

question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain why Victorian readers generally preferred borrowing novels from circulating libraries to buying them from booksellers
To show that the high cost of three-volume novels kept most Victorian readers from buying new fiction, leaving them dependent on circulating libraries
To suggest that a feature of Victorian fiction once credited to readers' tastes owed more to the interests of an intermediary
To trace how circulating libraries such as Mudie's grew in influence during the nineteenth century and then lost it after 1894

explanation.passage: Historians used to think Victorian novels came in three volumes because readers loved long stories. The passage then gives another explanation. The books were too expensive for most readers, so libraries bought them, and three volumes let libraries lend one novel to three people at once. Libraries pushed publishers to keep the format. When libraries stopped paying in 1894, the format disappeared, even though readers' tastes hadn't changed. The purpose is to replace a reader-taste explanation with a commercial one involving the libraries.
choices: Incorrect. The passage says novels were too expensive for most readers, but its point isn't why readers borrowed. That detail serves a larger argument about why the format existed.

Incorrect. This is accurate to the passage (the books cost more than a week's wages, and few readers bought them), but it is a supporting step, not the purpose. The text uses the high price to explain why libraries controlled the format and why the format reflected their interests, not readers' tastes.

Correct. The 'feature' is the three-volume format, once read as proof of readers' tastes. The 'intermediary' is the circulating libraries, which stood between publishers and readers and kept the format alive for their own lending needs. The 1894 collapse, with readers' tastes unchanged, clinches the point. The choice is abstract and avoids 'three volumes' and 'Mudie's'.

Incorrect. This is the strongest distractor, because the passage does mention the libraries' power and the 1894 turning point. But it uses those facts to explain the format, not to tell the libraries' history. It also never describes the libraries growing in influence.

passage.text: Cassava roots contain compounds that release cyanide, and so-called bitter varieties, which contain the most, must be grated, soaked, and pressed for hours before they are safe to eat. Agronomists long regarded the persistence of bitter cassava in Amazonian gardens as a puzzle—even as a failure of agricultural extension—given that sweet varieties requiring little processing were readily available. [u]Ethnobotanist Lucía Arévalo, however, found that the women who tended these gardens could name dozens of bitter varieties and chose among them deliberately.[/u] Their reasons, she reported, were practical: bitter roots are less often raided by peccaries and insects, they can be left in the ground for long periods without rotting, and the processed flour keeps for months—advantages that weigh more heavily in a household's calculations than the hours of labor processing demands.

question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It presents an observation suggesting that a practice described as puzzling reflects informed choice, setting up the account that follows.
It introduces the principal reason that bitter cassava continues to be grown, a reason that the rest of the text then qualifies.
It suggests that the persistence of bitter cassava owes more to cultural tradition than to the practical considerations that agronomists emphasized.
It provides the main evidence for the text's claim that bitter varieties are less vulnerable to pests and spoilage than sweet ones.

explanation.passage: Bitter cassava contains a poison and takes hours to prepare, so agronomists couldn't understand why Amazonian growers kept planting it when easy sweet varieties existed. The underlined sentence, which begins with 'however', reports that the women knew dozens of bitter varieties and chose among them on purpose. The next sentence then gives their practical reasons: protection from pests, long storage in the ground and long-keeping flour. So the underlined sentence turns the 'puzzle' into a knowing choice and leads into the explanation.
choices: Correct. 'However' marks a challenge to the agronomists' view. Knowing dozens of varieties and choosing 'deliberately' shows the practice is an informed decision, not a mistake, and the following sentence lays out the reasons. The choice describes this abstractly ('a practice described as puzzling', 'informed choice').

Incorrect. The underlined sentence gives no reason for growing bitter cassava; it shows only that the choice is deliberate. The reasons come in the next sentence, and the text doesn't qualify them. It ends by saying they outweigh the labor.

Incorrect. Knowing dozens of named varieties might sound like tradition, but the next sentence says the women's reasons 'were practical'. It also misstates the agronomists, who were puzzled by the practice rather than emphasizing practical reasons for it.

Incorrect. The facts about pests and spoilage come in the next sentence, as reasons the women gave. The underlined sentence is not evidence for them. It shows only that the women know many varieties and choose deliberately, which establishes that the practice is an informed choice before the reasons are given.

passage.label: Text 1
passage.text: In his 1966 essay “The Original Affluent Society,” anthropologist Marshall Sahlins challenged the image of foragers as people perpetually scrambling to survive. Drawing on Richard Lee's records of the Ju/'hoansi of the Kalahari, which showed adults spending roughly two to three hours a day hunting and gathering, Sahlins concluded that foragers met their needs with far less labor than workers in industrial societies, whose standard workweek was about forty hours.

passage.label: Text 2
passage.text: Later fieldworkers objected that Lee's early figures covered only the acquisition of food. Once the cracking of nuts, the butchering of game, the gathering of firewood, and the repair of tools were added, Ju/'hoansi adults were found to work about forty-two hours a week. Yet that total, unlike the standard industrial workweek, includes the equivalent of housework; studies of industrial households that add cooking, cleaning, and other domestic tasks to paid employment arrive at roughly sixty hours a week for an employed adult.

question: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Sahlins's conclusion in Text 1?
choices: By rejecting it, since foragers' total working hours turn out to be about equal to the length of a standard industrial workweek
By endorsing it, since the figures Sahlins relied on, if anything, overstated the amount of time foragers spent working
By limiting it to foragers in dry regions like the Kalahari, where food requires less processing than it does elsewhere
By suggesting that it may hold up even though the figures Sahlins relied on exaggerate how large foragers' advantage is

explanation.passage: Text 1: Sahlins compared foragers' 2–3 hours a day of food-getting with the 40-hour industrial workweek and concluded that foragers work much less. Text 2 does two things. First, it says the forager figure was too low, because once food processing and tool repair are counted, foragers work about 42 hours a week. Second, it says that's not a fair comparison either: the 42 hours include housework, while the 40-hour week doesn't, and industrial adults work about 60 hours once housework is added. So comparing like with like, foragers still work less, just not by as much as Sahlins thought.
choices: Incorrect. This stops halfway through Text 2. Forty-two hours does look close to the forty-hour week, but Text 2 then says the comparison is unfair because the 42 includes housework. Against the fairer figure of about 60 hours, foragers still work less.
Incorrect. This reverses Text 2's first point. Text 2 says Lee's early figures understated foragers' work by leaving out processing and tool repair; they didn't overstate it.
Incorrect. Neither text says that food in dry regions needs less processing, or compares the Kalahari with other places. This limitation is made up.

Correct. Text 2 shows Sahlins's numbers made the gap look too big: 2–3 hours a day versus 40 hours a week, when the comparable figures are about 42 versus about 60. But foragers still come out ahead, so his basic conclusion may survive. You need both texts: the 40-hour figure is in Text 1, and the corrected comparison is in Text 2.

passage.label: Text 1
passage.text: Historian Rolf Engelsing's influential thesis holds that a “reading revolution” transformed European reading in the second half of the eighteenth century. Before about 1750, he maintained, most readers read intensively: they owned a handful of books—a Bible, an almanac, a devotional work—and read them again and again, often aloud. Afterward, a growing middle class read extensively, consuming a steady stream of novels and periodicals, each read once and set aside.

passage.label: Text 2
passage.text: Letters that readers sent to Jean-Jacques Rousseau after the 1761 publication of his novel *Julie* complicate this picture. Correspondents describe reading the book repeatedly, reciting passages to their families, weeping over it, and treating it as a guide to the conduct of their own lives—habits strikingly like those once reserved for devotional texts. Yet many of the same writers mention, in passing, the dozens of other novels they had read and quickly forgotten.

question: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Engelsing's thesis?
choices: By arguing that novels, far from being read extensively, were read only in the intensive manner associated with devotional texts
By suggesting that it presents as successive two ways of reading that could in fact coexist in the habits of the same readers
By agreeing that it is supported by readers' letters, which show readers moving quickly through large numbers of novels
By objecting that it underestimates how many books readers owned before 1750, when devotional works circulated widely

explanation.passage: Text 1 describes Engelsing's 'reading revolution'. Before 1750 people read a few books over and over (intensive reading); after 1750 they read many books once each (extensive reading). One style replaced the other. Text 2 looks at letters from readers of Rousseau's novel *Julie*. They read it again and again, out loud and with deep emotion, which is intensive reading. But the same people also read dozens of other novels quickly, which is extensive reading. So both styles existed side by side in the same readers.
choices: Incorrect. This overcorrects. Text 2 shows *Julie* was read intensively, but the same readers 'read and quickly forgotten' dozens of other novels, which is extensive reading. So novels weren't read 'only' intensively.

Correct. Engelsing treats intensive and extensive reading as successive: one era, then the next. Text 2's letter-writers did both at once, rereading *Julie* devotedly while running through many other novels. The author would say the two modes coexisted rather than one replacing the other. The choice states this abstractly without naming the modes.

Incorrect. This uses only half of Text 2's evidence. The letters do mention many quickly read novels, but the main point is the intensive reading of *Julie*, which complicates Engelsing's thesis. Text 2 says the letters 'complicate this picture', not that they support it.
Incorrect. Text 2 says nothing about book ownership before 1750. This invents an objection outside the scope of both texts.

passage.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Vernalization is a requirement, found in some plants, for a prolonged period of cold before flowering can begin.
• Winter wheat is sown in autumn and must be vernalized, typically for six to eight weeks at temperatures between about 0°C and 10°C.
• Spring wheat is sown in spring and flowers without any period of cold.
• Winter wheat generally yields more grain per hectare than spring wheat.
• In 2022, plant geneticist Ruth Ndlovu grew 40 winter wheat varieties in chambers simulating winters 2°C and 4°C warmer than historical averages.
• The varieties whose vernalization requirement was met by the fewest cold days lost the least yield.

question: The student wants to explain why warmer winters may pose a risk to winter wheat that they do not pose to spring wheat. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Winter wheat is sown in autumn, whereas spring wheat is sown in spring, so only winter wheat is growing in the fields during the winter months.
In a 2022 study, the winter wheat varieties that needed the fewest cold days to be vernalized lost the least yield in simulated warmer winters.
Unlike spring wheat, winter wheat cannot flower until it has spent weeks at roughly 0°C to 10°C, a need that warmer winters could leave unmet.
Vernalization, a need for prolonged cold before flowering, applies to winter wheat, which generally yields more grain per hectare than spring wheat.

explanation.passage: The notes explain vernalization: some plants need a long cold spell before they can flower. Winter wheat needs one and spring wheat doesn't. The goal has two parts: explain why warmer winters could be a problem (the cause), and show why the problem applies to winter wheat but not spring wheat (the contrast). The right choice has to link the cold requirement to warm winters and set winter wheat against spring wheat.
choices: Incorrect. This is the main trap. It contrasts the two wheats and explains why only winter wheat experiences winter. But simply being in the ground during winter isn't a risk; the risk comes from needing cold to flower. It names the contrast but not the cause.

Incorrect. This reports a real finding about warmer winters, but it compares winter wheat varieties with one another, never mentions spring wheat, and doesn't explain why warmth is a problem in the first place.

Correct. It gives the cause (winter wheat must spend weeks at about 0–10°C before it can flower, which warmer winters might not provide) and the contrast ('Unlike spring wheat'). Both parts of the goal are met.

Incorrect. This defines vernalization and links it to winter wheat, but then turns to yield, which is irrelevant to the goal. It never connects the cold requirement to warmer winters or explains why spring wheat is not at risk.

passage.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Before the 1880s, newspaper type was set by hand, one metal letter at a time.
• A skilled hand compositor could set about 1,500 characters per hour.
• The Linotype machine, patented by Ottmar Mergenthaler in 1884, let an operator type on a keyboard to cast an entire line of type as a single metal bar, called a slug.
• A Linotype operator could set about 6,000 characters per hour.
• The *New York Tribune* first used the Linotype in 1886.
• By 1900, many large newspapers had expanded from 8 pages to 16 or more.

question: The student wants to quantify the Linotype's advantage over hand composition and explain how the machine achieved it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: A skilled hand compositor could set about 1,500 characters per hour, whereas a Linotype operator could set about 6,000 characters per hour.
Patented by Ottmar Mergenthaler in 1884, the Linotype let an operator use a keyboard to cast a whole line of type as a single metal slug.
By casting whole lines of type as single slugs, the Linotype let newspapers double in size, from 8 pages to 16 or more by 1900.
By casting whole lines from keyboard input instead of placing letters singly, the Linotype quadrupled a compositor's hourly output.

explanation.passage: The notes compare two ways of setting type for newspapers. By hand, letters were placed one at a time, about 1,500 characters an hour. The Linotype let an operator type on a keyboard and cast a whole line at once, about 6,000 characters an hour. The goal has two parts: give a number for the advantage (quantify) and say how the machine produced it (explain). The right choice needs both.
choices: Incorrect. This quantifies the advantage (1,500 vs. 6,000) but doesn't explain how the Linotype achieved it. It meets only one of the two conditions.
Incorrect. This explains how the machine worked but gives no figures, so it doesn't quantify the advantage. It meets only the other condition.

Incorrect. This is the main trap. It explains the mechanism and gives a number, but the number measures newspaper size, not the Linotype's advantage over hand composition. The notes also never say the Linotype caused papers to grow. They only list the two facts side by side.

Correct. It explains the mechanism (casting whole lines from a keyboard instead of setting letters one by one) and quantifies the result: 6,000 is four times 1,500, so output 'quadrupled'. You have to do the division to see that 'quadrupled' matches the notes.

passage.text: When asked to estimate their usual weekly working hours, employed Americans who report working 75 hours or more overstate their time on the job by roughly 25 hours, on average, relative to what detailed time diaries kept by the same people show. Sociologists have generally treated the diaries as the more trustworthy measure, since they record activities as the day unfolds rather than relying on a respondent's general impression. ______ the diaries are not free of error: people who are unusually busy on the day they are asked to keep one are more likely to decline, which would bias diary-based estimates downward.

question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: That said,
Indeed,
By contrast,
In particular,

explanation.passage: People who say they work very long hours overestimate by about 25 hours a week compared with their time diaries. The second sentence explains why researchers trust the diaries more. The third sentence turns around and admits a weakness in the diaries: very busy people tend not to fill them in, so diaries may undercount. The blank must signal a concession, a qualification of the praise for diaries just given.
choices: Correct. 'That said' introduces a qualification of what was just stated. The diaries are more trustworthy, but they aren't perfect. That is exactly the move from praising the diaries to admitting their flaw.

Incorrect. 'Indeed' reinforces or intensifies the previous point. But the sentence after the blank pushes against the previous one (diaries are trustworthy vs. diaries have errors), so it doesn't strengthen it.

Incorrect. 'By contrast' sets up a difference between two things. But the sentence after the blank doesn't set the diaries against something else. It admits the diaries share a weakness (error) with the self-reports, which qualifies the praise just given rather than contrasting with it.
Incorrect. 'In particular' introduces a specific case of a general point just made. The diaries' error isn't a specific example of why they are trustworthy; it points the other way.

passage.text: By the late 1960s, American seed companies had adopted a shortcut for producing hybrid maize. Rather than paying workers to pull the pollen-bearing tassels from the plants designated as mothers, they bred those plants to carry “Texas” cytoplasm, an inherited cellular trait that renders maize pollen-sterile. The shortcut proved so convenient that roughly 85 percent of the nation's maize came to carry this single cytoplasm. ______ a crop that farmers took to be genetically diverse—it comprised hundreds of distinct hybrids—was uniform in one critical respect, and when a fungal strain to which Texas cytoplasm happened to be acutely vulnerable spread in 1970, it destroyed some 15 percent of the harvest.

question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Even so,
Moreover,
In effect,
For instance,

explanation.passage: To save labor, seed companies gave the mother plants a trait (Texas cytoplasm) that made them unable to produce pollen. So many companies did this that about 85 percent of US maize carried the same cytoplasm. The sentence after the blank restates what that meant in practice: hundreds of different hybrids looked diverse, but they all shared one trait, and when a fungus attacked that trait, the damage was huge. The transition must signal that the sentence spells out the practical meaning of the previous fact.
choices: Incorrect. 'Even so' signals that something happened despite what came before. But the crop's uniformity doesn't happen in spite of 85 percent sharing one cytoplasm; it's what that sharing amounts to. The word 'took to be… diverse' may tempt you toward a contrast, but that contrast lies inside the sentence, not between the two sentences.

Incorrect. 'Moreover' adds a new, separate point. The uniformity isn't a new fact on top of the 85 percent figure; it's that same fact viewed from another angle. (The 1970 epidemic is new, but it's in the second half of the sentence, after the restatement.)

Correct. 'In effect' introduces what something amounts to in practice. Eighty-five percent sharing one cytoplasm meant that, despite its apparent diversity, the crop was effectively uniform in one critical way. The sentence reinterprets the previous fact and then shows its consequence.
Incorrect. 'For instance' introduces an example of a general claim. The sentence after the blank isn't one example of the 85 percent figure; it describes the whole crop.

intro: The following text is from Henry James's 1880 novel *Washington Square*. The narrator is introducing a character.

passage.text: During a portion of the first half of the present century, and more particularly during the latter part of it, there flourished and practised in the city of New York a physician who enjoyed perhaps an exceptional share of the [u]consideration[/u] which, in the United States, has always been bestowed upon distinguished members of the medical profession. This profession in America has constantly been held in honour, and more successfully than elsewhere has put forward a claim to the epithet of “liberal.”

question: As used in the text, what does the word “consideration” most nearly mean?
choices: Thoughtfulness
Esteem
Deliberation
Compensation

explanation.passage: The narrator introduces a successful New York doctor. He says this doctor enjoyed an unusually large 'share of the consideration' that Americans have always 'bestowed upon' distinguished doctors. The next sentence explains: the medical profession in America has 'constantly been held in honour'. So 'consideration' here is something society gives to respected doctors, and the next sentence calls it honour.
choices: Incorrect. This is the everyday sense of 'consideration' (being considerate or kind to others). Society doesn't bestow 'thoughtfulness' on a profession, and the next sentence talks about honour, not kindness.
Correct. 'Consideration' here is an older sense meaning high regard or respect. Society 'bestowed' it on distinguished doctors, and the next sentence restates it as being 'held in honour'.

Incorrect. 'Deliberation' (careful thought before deciding) is another common sense of 'consideration', as in 'under consideration'. But a doctor can't enjoy a 'share' of deliberation bestowed by society.

Incorrect. This is tempting because 'consideration' can mean payment ('for a small consideration'), and 'share' and 'bestowed' sound like money. But the next sentence explains the idea as honour, not income.

passage.text: In 2017, Colin Donihue and colleagues had just finished measuring *Anolis scriptus* lizards on two small islands in the Turks and Caicos when Hurricanes Irma and Maria struck. Returning weeks later, they found that the survivors had, relative to body size, larger toe pads and longer forelimbs than the pre-storm population—differences readily attributed to selection for a stronger grip—but also shorter hindlimbs, a change that is puzzling if survival depended on grip alone, since hindlimbs help a lizard hold on as well. In a follow-up test, lizards placed on a narrow perch and exposed to steadily rising wind held on chiefly with their forelimbs, while their hindlimbs, lifted from the perch, swung outward into the airflow. Taken together, these observations suggest that ______

question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the survivors' hindlimbs, like their toe pads and forelimbs, were favored because they let lizards keep a firmer hold on perches in high winds.
the survivors' shorter hindlimbs were most likely an incidental consequence of selection for longer forelimbs rather than a trait favored in itself.
shorter hindlimbs may have been favored less for any part they played in gripping than for leaving less of the body exposed to dislodging forces.
lizards with shorter hindlimbs probably survived by abandoning exposed perches for sheltered ground before the storms reached their full strength.

explanation.passage: Researchers happened to measure island lizards just before two hurricanes, then measured the survivors. Two changes make easy sense: bigger toe pads and longer front legs help a lizard grip. The third change, shorter back legs, is the puzzle, because the passage says back legs help with gripping too. The wind test solves it: in strong wind the lizards held on with their front legs while their back legs lifted off and swung out into the wind. So you need to work out what shorter back legs would do for a lizard whose back legs are flapping in the wind rather than gripping.
choices: Incorrect. This lumps the hindlimbs in with the toe pads and forelimbs, which is exactly what the passage warns against. The wind test shows the hindlimbs were not holding on at all; they had lifted off the perch. And if grip were the reason, longer hindlimbs, not shorter ones, would have been favored.

Incorrect. This sounds like a sophisticated biological explanation, which makes it tempting, but the passage never says the two traits are linked in development. It also ignores the wind test, which gives a direct reason shorter hindlimbs would help on their own. It brings in an outside explanation the passage gives no support for.

Correct. In the wind test the hindlimbs weren't gripping; they were swinging out into the airflow, where they would catch wind like a sail. Shorter hindlimbs catch less wind, so they would be less likely to pull a lizard off its perch. You have to supply that reasoning step yourself. The choice is hedged ('may have been favored') and avoids the passage's own words such as 'wind' and 'airflow'.

Incorrect. The passage says nothing about where lizards sheltered, and the follow-up test was about lizards holding on to a perch in wind. This invents a behavior to explain the trait instead of using the evidence the passage gives.

passage.text: During the 1996 Summer Olympics, Atlanta officials—anticipating gridlock—expanded public transit, encouraged staggered work hours, and closed much of downtown to private cars, measures that cut weekday morning traffic by about 22 percent. Over the same 17 days, Michael Friedman and colleagues found, peak ozone concentrations fell by more than a quarter, and children's emergency visits for asthma, a condition that ozone is known to aggravate, fell by roughly 40 percent relative to the weeks before and after the Games. A skeptic might propose that families, faced with closed roads and crowds, simply put off trips to clinics and hospitals while the Games went on; over the same period, however, children's emergency visits for conditions other than asthma held essentially steady. This last result suggests that ______

question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: an explanation that would apply equally to every kind of childhood illness cannot account for the drop in asthma visits.
the transit measures reduced asthma visits by lowering ozone rather than by reducing the other pollutants found in vehicle exhaust.
the reduction in traffic, rather than weather or any other factor, was entirely responsible for the decline in ozone during the Games.
the decline in asthma visits was caused by the drop in ozone rather than by any change in how often families sought medical care for their children.

explanation.passage: Atlanta cut traffic during the 1996 Olympics, and in the same weeks ozone (an air pollutant) and children's asthma emergencies both dropped. A skeptic offers another explanation: maybe families just avoided going to the doctor because the city was crowded and roads were closed. The last sentence tests that idea. If families were avoiding doctors, visits for every kind of illness should have dropped, but visits for other conditions stayed the same. The question asks what that 'last result' shows, so the answer must be about the skeptic's alternative, not about traffic or ozone in general.
choices: Correct. The skeptic's explanation (families avoiding clinics) would affect visits for every illness, not just asthma. Because visits for other conditions held steady, that kind of across-the-board explanation can't account for the asthma drop. The choice never mentions families, clinics or the Games; you have to see that 'an explanation that would apply equally to every kind of childhood illness' describes the skeptic's idea.

Incorrect. This is a strong distractor because ozone is the pollutant the passage names. But the 'last result' (steady visits for other conditions) only rules out the skeptic's explanation. It says nothing about ozone versus other exhaust pollutants, since the passage never measured those. The choice is over-specified.

Incorrect. This overreaches ('entirely responsible'), and it answers a different question. The steady non-asthma visits concern whether families avoided care; they tell us nothing about what caused the ozone drop. The passage never rules out weather.

Incorrect. This is half right, which makes it tempting. The steady non-asthma visits do rule out the idea that families stopped seeking care. But they don't prove that ozone was the cause: the passage shows only that ozone and asthma visits fell at the same time, and other pollutants or factors could also have changed. 'Was caused by the drop in ozone' claims more than the last result shows.

passage.text: In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, as maize became a staple food for poor farmers in southern Europe and, later, the American South, outbreaks of pellagra—a disease now known to result from a deficiency of niacin, one of the B vitamins—became widespread. In Mexico and Central America, by contrast, where maize had been the dietary mainstay for thousands of years, pellagra was rare. There, maize was traditionally simmered in an alkaline solution of lime or wood ash before being ground, a process called nixtamalization that frees niacin otherwise bound in the grain in a form the body cannot absorb. European growers adopted the crop but not this method of preparing it, which suggests that ______

question: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: maize grown in Europe contained less niacin than did the maize grown in Mexico and Central America at the time.
Mesoamerican cooks developed nixtamalization specifically to protect themselves against the effects of pellagra.
pellagra could have been prevented in Europe only if farmers there had eaten considerably less maize than they did.
the illness that followed maize's spread owed less to the grain itself than to the way it was prepared for eating.

explanation.passage: Pellagra is a disease caused by too little niacin, a vitamin. When maize (corn) became a staple in Europe and the American South, pellagra spread. But in Mexico and Central America, where people had eaten maize far longer, pellagra was rare. The difference is preparation: there, maize was cooked in an alkaline solution (nixtamalization), which makes its niacin usable by the body. Europeans took the crop without that step. So you need to infer what caused the disease in Europe.
choices: Incorrect. This brings in a different cause, the niacin content of the grain, which the passage never mentions. The passage says the niacin is present but 'bound' in a form the body can't absorb unless the maize is treated. This is the most tempting wrong answer because it mentions niacin.
Incorrect. This adds a motive the passage doesn't give. The passage describes what nixtamalization does, not why people invented it. They may never have known about pellagra at all.

Incorrect. 'Only if' is too strong, and it misses the passage's point. Mesoamericans ate maize as their main food and rarely got pellagra, so eating less maize was not the only way to prevent it; preparing it differently worked.

Correct. Both regions ate lots of maize, but only the region that skipped nixtamalization had widespread pellagra. So the problem was mainly how the maize was prepared, not the maize itself. The choice states this abstractly without repeating 'nixtamalization' or 'niacin'.

passage.text: Beginning in 1959, geneticist Dmitry Belyaev and, later, his colleague Lyudmila Trut bred silver foxes on a Siberian fur farm, allowing only the least fearful individuals of each generation to reproduce. Within about ten generations, some of the tame foxes had developed piebald (white-patched) coats, floppy ears, and curled tails—traits common in domestic dogs but rare in wild foxes—even though the researchers had never selected for appearance. Because these traits became markedly more frequent in the tame line as the experiment went on, Trut has argued that selection for tameness by itself drove their spread, a conclusion widely cited as evidence that domestication tends to produce a predictable suite of physical traits in whatever species undergoes it.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Trut's conclusion?
choices: Piebald coats had occasionally been recorded among the farm-bred foxes from which the experiment's founders came, decades before the experiment began.
Foxes from the same stock, bred without regard to temperament, showed rises in those traits over the same period comparable to the tame line's.
Foxes bred in a parallel line for aggression toward humans showed no increase in piebald coats, floppy ears, or curled tails over the same generations.
Foxes in the tame line had lower levels of stress hormones than unselected foxes, a difference that appeared within the first few generations of breeding.

explanation.passage: Researchers bred foxes, letting only the tamest ones have offspring. Over generations, dog-like traits (patchy coats, floppy ears, curly tails) became more common, though nobody chose foxes for their looks. Trut concludes that choosing for tameness alone caused these traits to spread. Notice the exact claim: it is about the traits becoming more frequent, and it credits tameness 'by itself'. To weaken it, you need evidence that the traits would have spread even without selection for tameness.
choices: Incorrect. This is the main trap, and it is based on a real debate. It shows the traits weren't brand new. But Trut's claim is that the traits became more common, and a trait already present at low levels can still be spread by selection. The finding doesn't break the link between tameness and the increase.

Correct. This removes the variable the conclusion depends on. If foxes from the same stock that were never selected for tameness gained these traits just as much, then something else (farm conditions, or the stock's own genes) explains the spread, not selection for tameness.
Incorrect. This supports Trut. If foxes selected for the opposite temperament didn't develop the traits, that strengthens the case that tameness is what matters.

Incorrect. True-but-not-the-task. Lower stress hormones in tame foxes describe one effect of selecting for tameness, and might even suggest how tameness could change appearance. It does nothing to show the traits would have spread without that selection.

passage.text: When a congested highway is widened, traffic speeds typically improve at first and then decline, often to near their original levels within a few years. Analyzing U.S. metropolitan areas between 1983 and 2003, economists Gilles Duranton and Matthew Turner found that total vehicle-kilometers traveled rose almost exactly in proportion to added interstate lane-kilometers—a regularity they called “the fundamental law of road congestion.” They argue that the regularity reflects new demand rather than diverted or population-driven traffic: the added traffic consists largely of trips that would not otherwise have been made at all, rather than of trips merely shifted from other roads, and the effect appears whether or not a metropolitan area's population is growing.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Duranton and Turner's explanation?
choices: Traffic on roads running parallel to newly widened highways fell sharply after widening, by amounts roughly matching the increases on the highways.
In fast-growing metropolitan areas, driving rose in proportion to added lane-kilometers, with most of the increase coming from trips not previously made.
Commuters surveyed after a highway was widened reported shorter travel times during the first year but longer travel times by the third year.
Where populations were stable, added lanes were followed by proportional rises in total driving, very little of it offset by declines on nearby roads.

explanation.passage: Widening a highway helps traffic at first, but within a few years it's about as slow as before. Duranton and Turner found that driving grows in step with new lanes. Their explanation has two parts: (1) the extra traffic is mostly new trips, not trips shifted over from other roads, and (2) this happens even where population isn't growing. A finding that 'most directly supports' the explanation should back up both parts.
choices: Incorrect. This works against part 1. If parallel roads lost about as much traffic as the highway gained, the extra highway traffic was diverted from other roads, not new trips. A careless reader may see 'more traffic on the widened highway' and think it fits.

Incorrect. This is the strongest distractor: it confirms part 1 (new trips). But it describes only fast-growing areas, so it can't show the effect happens 'whether or not' population is growing. There, growth itself could explain the extra driving. It covers only one half of the explanation.

Incorrect. True-but-not-the-task. This matches the pattern described in the first sentence (speeds improve, then decline), but it says nothing about where the extra traffic comes from or about population, which is what the explanation is about.

Correct. Stable populations take care of part 2: the rise in driving can't be put down to more residents. 'Very little of it offset by declines on nearby roads' takes care of part 1: the traffic wasn't just shifted from elsewhere, so it must be new driving. This is the only choice that covers both parts.

passage.text: In “Crossing Brooklyn Ferry” (1856), Walt Whitman addresses people who will ride the ferry between Brooklyn and Manhattan long after his death. Critics often observe that the poem bridges this gap in time through shared sensation—the same river, the same sky, the same crowds seen from the deck—yet the poem goes further than that, claiming kinship with future riders not only in what they will enjoy but also in their moral and spiritual shortcomings, as when Whitman writes, ______

question: Which quotation from “Crossing Brooklyn Ferry” most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: “Just as you feel when you look on the river and sky, so I felt, / Just as any of you is one of a living crowd, I was one of a crowd”
“What is it then between us? / What is the count of the scores or hundreds of years between us? / Whatever it is, it avails not—distance avails not, and place avails not”
“It is not upon you alone the dark patches fall, / The dark threw its patches down upon me also, / The best I had done seem'd to me blank and suspicious”
“And you that shall cross from shore to shore years hence are more to me, and more in my meditations, than you might suppose”

explanation.passage: Whitman speaks directly to people who will ride the same ferry in the future. The passage first mentions what critics usually notice: Whitman connects with future riders through shared sights and feelings. Then it makes a stronger claim: he also connects with them through shared faults, their 'moral and spiritual shortcomings'. The word 'yet… further than that' tells you the right quotation must go beyond shared sensations and show Whitman admitting he has the same flaws or doubts that his readers will have. Three of the choices express a bond with future riders, so the deciding question is which one makes that bond a matter of shared faults.
choices: Incorrect. This is the main trap. It's a strong statement of kinship with future riders, but the kinship is in sensation (looking at the river and sky, being in a crowd), which is the critics' point the passage says the poem goes beyond. It shows nothing about shortcomings.

Incorrect. This is a strong statement of kinship across time: Whitman says the 'hundreds of years' between him and his readers don't matter ('avails not' means 'makes no difference'). But it claims a connection in general, not a shared weakness. Nothing in it concerns moral or spiritual shortcomings, so it doesn't go beyond what the critics already observe.

Correct. Whitman tells the reader that the 'dark patches' do not fall on 'you alone' but fell on him 'also'. The third line makes the metaphor clear: even his best work seemed to him 'blank and suspicious', a confession of self-doubt. This is kinship in shortcomings, exactly what the claim needs, though you have to read 'dark patches' as a metaphor.

Incorrect. Tempting, because it speaks to future riders and says they matter deeply to him. But caring about readers is not the same as sharing their failings; the line expresses his attention to them, not a common weakness.

passage.text: A long-standing account traces the restaurant to the French Revolution: as aristocrats fled Paris after 1789, the story goes, the chefs they left behind, needing work, opened public dining rooms that brought noble cuisine to paying customers. Historian Rebecca Spang does not deny that some such chefs went into business, but she rejects the account as an explanation of where restaurants came from. In her reconstruction, the first Parisian restaurants sold “restaurants”—restorative broths—to customers who considered themselves of delicate health, and what set these establishments apart from older eating houses was not their food but their format: diners sat at separate tables, chose from a menu, and ate when they wished, rather than taking a fixed meal at a shared table at a set hour.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly explain why Spang rejects the long-standing account?
choices: Guidebooks to Paris from the early 1780s already listed many eating houses run in the format the text identifies as distinctive of restaurants.
Several of the most celebrated Paris restaurants of the 1790s were founded by chefs who had previously cooked in the households of noble families.
The number of restaurants operating in Paris increased several times over during the decade that followed the outbreak of the Revolution in 1789.
Parisian physicians recommended restorative broths to patients suffering from a wide range of ailments throughout much of the eighteenth century.

explanation.passage: The common story says restaurants were invented after the French Revolution (1789) by chefs who lost their jobs when their noble employers fled. Spang agrees some chefs did open restaurants, but she denies that this explains where restaurants came from. For her, the restaurant was defined by its format (separate tables, a menu, eating whenever you liked), and it started as a place selling healthy broths. To explain why she rejects the story, a finding should show that the restaurant, as she defines it, existed before the Revolution could have caused it.
choices: Correct. If guidebooks from the early 1780s, years before 1789, already listed many eating houses with the separate-tables, menu, any-hour format, then restaurants existed before the Revolution and can't have been invented by chefs it put out of work. The choice never calls these places restaurants; you have to connect 'the format… distinctive of restaurants' to the passage's last sentence.
Incorrect. This supports the long-standing account, and it's the part Spang already concedes ('does not deny that some such chefs went into business'). It can't explain why she rejects the account.
Incorrect. Rapid growth after 1789 fits the long-standing account at least as well as Spang's. It shows restaurants spread after the Revolution, not that they began before it.

Incorrect. This connects to the word 'restaurants' meaning restorative broths, so it looks relevant. But broths being prescribed says nothing about when the restaurant as an institution, with its distinctive format, appeared. Broth could have been sold or made at home long before any restaurant existed.

passage.text: In the 1990s, Dutch traffic engineer Hans Monderman began redesigning village intersections by removing traffic lights, signs, and even the curbs that separated roadway from sidewalk. The approach, later termed “shared space,” struck many observers as reckless, but it rested on a behavioral hypothesis: stripped of the cues that tell them who has the right of way, drivers would feel uncertain, and it is this uncertainty—rather than any physical obstacle placed in their path—that would lead them to slow down and to negotiate passage with pedestrians and cyclists through eye contact. Monderman's critics, for their part, have argued that wherever shared-space schemes have reduced speeds, the reductions owe more to narrowed lanes and changes in paving than to anything going on in drivers' minds.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Monderman's hypothesis?
choices: Crash rates at redesigned intersections fell in the years after the changes, even though the total volume of traffic passing through them stayed about the same.
Drivers slowed sharply after a redesign that left the roadway's width and surface unaltered, and video showed them glancing toward pedestrians far more often.
At intersections where planters and raised paving were added along with the removal of signs, drivers slowed more than where signs alone were removed.
Drivers surveyed after redesigns reported feeling less certain about who had the right of way, and many described the new intersections as stressful.

explanation.passage: Monderman removed traffic lights, signs and curbs from intersections. His hypothesis: without those cues drivers feel unsure, and that uncertainty (not physical barriers) makes them slow down and make eye contact with pedestrians. His critics say any slowing really comes from physical changes like narrower lanes or new paving. So the best support must show drivers slowing and watching pedestrians when nothing physical about the road changed, which rules out the critics' explanation.
choices: Incorrect. Fewer crashes is a good outcome, but it doesn't show how it happened: whether drivers slowed, or whether uncertainty rather than physical changes was responsible. It speaks to the scheme's results, not the hypothesis's mechanism.

Correct. The road's width and surface stayed the same, which rules out the critics' physical explanation. Drivers still slowed sharply, and they looked toward pedestrians far more often, which matches the eye-contact negotiation the hypothesis predicts. It covers the slowing, the cause and the negotiation.
Incorrect. This supports the critics. If adding physical features (planters, raised paving) made drivers slow more, that points to physical changes, not uncertainty, as the main cause.

Incorrect. This is half the hypothesis. It shows drivers felt uncertain, but not that the uncertainty made them slow down or negotiate with pedestrians. Feeling stressed is not the same as driving more carefully.

passage.text: The legal limit for annual mean nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) concentration in the city of Haldemar is 40 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³). After a low-emission zone restricting older diesel vehicles took effect in the city center in 2019, officials judged the zone's effect at each monitoring site by the site's “excess”—the amount by which its annual mean exceeded 40 µg/m³—and counted the zone as effective at a site only if that excess shrank by at least half between 2018 and 2021. Reviewing data from two sites inside the zone and two outside it, a researcher concludes that, by the officials' criterion, the zone was effective at at least one site beyond its boundaries.

figure.title: Annual Mean NO₂ Concentration at Four Haldemar Monitoring Sites

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the researcher's conclusion?
choices: At Riverside, the annual mean fell from 44 µg/m³ to 39 µg/m³, which brought the site below the city's legal limit.
At North Ring, the annual mean fell from 52 µg/m³ to 47 µg/m³, a larger decline than the one recorded at Eastgate.
At Eastgate, the annual mean fell from 47 µg/m³ to 43 µg/m³, which more than halved its excess over the limit.
At Central Market, the annual mean fell by 12 µg/m³, which was the largest decline recorded at any of the four sites.

explanation.passage: The passage sets up a special test. A site's 'excess' is how far its pollution level is above 40. The zone counts as 'effective' at a site only if that excess was at least cut in half from 2018 to 2021. The researcher says the zone was effective at one or more sites outside the zone. So look only at the two outside sites, North Ring and Eastgate, and work out their excess each year. North Ring: 52 − 40 = 12, then 47 − 40 = 7; 7 is more than half of 12, so it doesn't count. Eastgate: 47 − 40 = 7, then 43 − 40 = 3; 3 is less than half of 7, so it counts.
choices: Incorrect. Riverside did meet the officials' test (its excess went from 4 to 0), but it is inside the zone. The conclusion is about sites outside the zone, so this is the wrong group of sites.

Incorrect. This is the main trap. North Ring is outside the zone and its drop (5) was larger than Eastgate's (4). But the test is about the share of the excess removed. North Ring's excess went from 12 to 7, a cut of less than half, so by the officials' criterion the zone was not effective there.

Correct. Eastgate is outside the zone. Its excess fell from 7 (47 − 40) to 3 (43 − 40), which is less than half of what it was, so the site meets the officials' criterion. That is the evidence the conclusion needs.

Incorrect. The numbers are right (58 − 46 = 12, the biggest drop), but Central Market is inside the zone, so it can't show an effect beyond the zone's boundaries. It describes the graph accurately without addressing the conclusion.

passage.text: Marine threespine sticklebacks are covered with bony armor plates, whereas most lake populations descended from them are “low-plated.” After two Alaskan lakes, Loberg and Cheney, were cleared of fish and then recolonized by marine sticklebacks, biologists sampled each lake every two years and recorded the percentage of low-plated fish. They regard a population as having shifted to the lake form once low-plated fish make up a majority of a sample, and as having stabilized once that percentage changes by less than 5 percentage points between consecutive samples. A student claims that the Loberg population shifted to the lake form before the Cheney population did but stabilized later than the Cheney population.

figure.title: Low-Plated Sticklebacks in Two Recolonized Alaskan Lakes

question: Which choice best describes the extent to which the data in the graph support the student's claim?
choices: They support the first part but not the second, since Loberg's percentage changed by under 5 points between 1998 and 2000, which Cheney's did only between 2000 and 2002.
They support both parts, since Loberg's percentage first exceeded 50 in 1996, earlier than Cheney's did, and was still rising in 2002, when Cheney's had nearly leveled off.
They support neither part, since Cheney's percentage was higher than Loberg's in 1990 and Loberg's was higher than Cheney's in every sample taken from 1994 onward.
They support the second part but not the first, since Cheney's percentage exceeded 50 in 1996, the same year that Loberg's did, and continued rising for longer.

explanation.passage: The passage defines two milestones. 'Shifted' means low-plated fish are more than 50% of a sample. 'Stabilized' means the percentage changes by less than 5 points from one sample to the next. The student makes two claims: Loberg shifted first, and Loberg stabilized later. Check each. Shifted: Loberg first passes 50 in 1996 (61); Cheney first passes 50 in 1998 (66; in 1996 it was only 48). So Loberg shifted first, which is true. Stabilized: Loberg changes by 14 (1996–98), then 4 (1998–2000), so it stabilizes in 2000. Cheney changes by 18, then 6 (1998–2000), then 2 (2000–02), so it stabilizes in 2002. Loberg stabilized earlier, so the second claim is false.
